course.title: Prompt Engineering
course.description:
Practical skills for working with generative AI in academic and business tasks — no programming required. You use chatbots, define a task and its success criteria, design prompts, improve answers with follow-ups, choose a prompting strategy and evaluate the result.

You practise on two connected retail cases built on a 200-transaction CSV: a regional sales visualisation and a business investigation that ends in an action plan. Along the way you verify every figure and claim, build reusable workflows, and apply privacy, security and documentation habits.

14 periods in five modules, following one cycle: **Define → Design → Execute → Evaluate → Refine**. Every period has a lesson, practice questions with feedback on the exact misconception behind a wrong answer, and flashcards for spaced review. The lecture notes, slides and activity sheets are attached.

misconceptions.name: Supplies something other than the actual task evidence
misconceptions.description: Offers a filename, a cover image or an unrelated file when the task needs the values themselves. A name or a picture identifies a thing without containing its data, so the chatbot has nothing to analyse. Typical sign: "I mentioned the file, so it knows what is in it."

misconceptions.name: Assumes the chatbot can see or compute on a file it has not received
misconceptions.description: Believes the tool has read a file because it was mentioned, or that it can run a calculation on data it never got. Without file access, any regional total it gives is invented. Typical sign: accepting a table of numbers without checking that the file was attached and opened.

misconceptions.name: Chooses an output format that does not fit the question
misconceptions.description: Picks a narrative, a spoken or a decorative format for a task that asks for exact values or a comparison. The reader then cannot see or check the answer easily. Typical sign: asking for an essay when four numbers need ranking.

misconceptions.name: Gives the approval or the accountability to the AI or a tool
misconceptions.description: Treats the chatbot, a template or a chart generator as the party that signs off a recommendation. These tools can draft and format but they cannot be accountable for a decision. Typical sign: "the AI wrote it, so it has been approved."

misconceptions.name: Treats a polished or fluent report as proof of understanding
misconceptions.description: Judges work by how it looks, such as cover design, headings or paragraph count, instead of by whether the person can explain and repeat it. AI can make presentation strong with no understanding behind it. Typical sign: "the report looks professional, so they must know the method."

misconceptions.name: Confuses the stages of the Define, Design, Execute, Evaluate, Refine cycle
misconceptions.description: Labels a step by the action it looks like instead of by its purpose in the cycle. For example, any new request looks like "execute". The stage is decided by why you do it: setting the task, writing the request, running it, checking it, or changing it after a check.

misconceptions.name: Misunderstands what a token is
misconceptions.description: Takes a token to be a data value, an axis, an approval or a record, instead of a piece of text that the model processes. This hides the point that the model works with text patterns, not guaranteed facts. Typical sign: connecting "token" with something in the data.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up the kind of AI error that has occurred
misconceptions.description: Files an invented source under display, layout or ordering problems. A fabricated citation is missing evidence, not poor presentation, so a layout fix cannot repair it. Typical sign: reaching for a formatting fix when a fact or source is the problem.

misconceptions.name: Reads a cause or a fact into a plain comparison of totals
misconceptions.description: Takes a low or high recorded total as proof of a reason such as weak demand, or keeps an explanation as a finding because it sounds sensible. A table of totals shows a comparison, not what caused it. Typical sign: the words "because", "caused" or "proves" next to a total.

misconceptions.name: Fills a gap in the data with a guess
misconceptions.description: Replaces a missing fact with something that sounds likely, such as fewer stores, low profit, a date or a guessed explanation. The file does not hold that information, so the new claim is as unsupported as the old one. Typical sign: swapping one unsupported explanation for another.

misconceptions.name: Lets the AI certify or approve its own answer
misconceptions.description: Asks the system that produced an answer to confirm it is correct, or to approve the conclusion. Its confirmation comes from the same patterns that produced the answer, so it is not independent evidence. Typical sign: "I asked the AI and it says it is right."

misconceptions.name: Rejects a whole length or format or a whole answer instead of checking the claim
misconceptions.description: Overcorrects by deciding that long answers, tables or charts cannot be trusted, or by throwing out everything without checking. This wastes good evidence and still does not tell you what is true. Typical sign: a blanket rule about output type or about "never using AI".

misconceptions.name: Accepts a source, a number or an explanation because it sounds or looks credible
misconceptions.description: Treats fluent wording, a tidy citation, a plausible figure or repetition as proof. None of these shows that a source exists or a calculation was done. Typical sign: not opening the link, not recalculating, "it sounds right".

misconceptions.name: Starts with presentation details before the decision is clear
misconceptions.description: Chooses colours, headings or a persona before knowing what decision the analysis supports. The presentation then drives the work instead of the problem. Typical sign: "first let me decide how the report will look."

misconceptions.name: Asks a question the available data cannot answer
misconceptions.description: Poses a question about profit, targets, growth or dates when the file holds only net sales by region and transaction. The result is a guess presented as an analysis. Typical sign: a good question that no column can support.

misconceptions.name: Uses a vague or tone-based goal instead of a checkable criterion
misconceptions.description: Writes "be useful", "sound confident" or "act as an expert" as if they defined success. None of them tells you whether the result passes. Typical sign: a brief with no observable condition that someone else could test.

misconceptions.name: Adds wording or polish instead of the missing information
misconceptions.description: Reacts to a weak brief by lengthening it, adding background or improving the format, when the real gap is a missing audience, a missing input or a missing column. More words do not supply what is absent. Typical sign: revising the style while the requirement stays unstated.

misconceptions.name: Misses that a word such as "best" hides a choice of metric
misconceptions.description: Treats "best", "top" or "performing" as if it named one measure, or blames some other feature of the request. In fact it could mean sales, margin, growth or volume, and each needs different evidence. Typical sign: a ranking with no stated measure.

misconceptions.name: Reuses the same criteria for different decisions, or strips the context away
misconceptions.description: Assumes that a shared dataset means shared requirements, so the same success test is reused, the context is removed, or the tool picks the objective. The criteria should follow the actual decision. Typical sign: one standard brief for every manager.

misconceptions.name: Leaves the task, metric or grouping unnamed
misconceptions.description: Believes a prompt can stay general ('study this file', 'consider everything', a more formal tone) and the chatbot will work out the analysis. It cannot: without a named metric, grouping and output, the model guesses and you have nothing specific to check. Sign: the prompt has no column name and no format.

misconceptions.name: Expects a role, persona or polished tone to supply the missing task details
misconceptions.description: Treats 'You are an expert...' or flattering titles as if they gave the model skill, knowledge of the retailer or accuracy. A role sets a voice at most; it does not name the measure, supply data or make a total correct. Sign: the prompt spends words on who the model is and none on what to calculate.

misconceptions.name: Treats a longer or more elaborate prompt as a better prompt
misconceptions.description: Assumes more personas, examples, headings or context always improve the result, or that a revised long prompt must beat a short one that already works. Extra text can add conflicting instructions or false assumptions. Sign: words are added without testing whether the output changed.

misconceptions.name: Thinks examples or description can stand in for the source data
misconceptions.description: Believes that describing the task, or showing worked examples, gives the model what it needs even though the actual CSV or table is not supplied. Examples show a pattern; only the data supplies figures. Sign: the prompt has samples but no attachment or pasted table.

misconceptions.name: Confuses which prompt function a piece of text performs
misconceptions.description: Mixes up instruction, context, input, output specification, constraint and role, or treats a data field as a rule. The functions do different jobs: the instruction says what to do, the output says what shape to return, a constraint limits what may be claimed. Sign: labelling a column name as a constraint, or identity as an instruction.

misconceptions.name: Fills a gap in the data with a plausible guess
misconceptions.description: When the file lacks something (currency, profit, dates) the learner keeps a plausible default, asks for an estimate or swaps in another measure. The prompt must respect what the source contains and say the rest is unspecified. Sign: 'dollars', 'profit' or 'monthly' appear although the CSV has no such field.

misconceptions.name: Believes one provider's layout is mandatory or automatically better
misconceptions.description: Thinks a single named template, or the layout with more headings, produces better answers. OpenAI-, Google- and Anthropic-style layouts group the same needs differently; none is required. Sign: choosing a layout by label or length instead of testing outputs against one rubric.

misconceptions.name: Misdefines what a follow-up prompt is
misconceptions.description: Thinks a follow-up is a file, a contract or a check on the data, rather than a further instruction that builds on an answer already in the conversation. A follow-up refines; it does not verify. Sign: calling a follow-up 'a replacement for checking' or describing it as something produced before the task.

misconceptions.name: Sends a vague or unrelated follow-up instead of naming the defect and the fix
misconceptions.description: Reaches for 'make it better', more adjectives, a new dataset or a different KPI instead of naming the one observed weakness and the change wanted. Such follow-ups cannot be assessed and often change what is being compared. Sign: the follow-up does not say what was wrong with the last answer.

misconceptions.name: Adds context or detail that does not serve the reader or the decision
misconceptions.description: Includes details that change nothing about the task (office decor, a tool's avatar, jargon, code) or removes the business question, instead of audience, purpose and length. Context counts only if it changes the answer. Sign: the added sentence could be deleted without any change to the result.

misconceptions.name: Accepts or hides a revised answer without re-checking it
misconceptions.description: Treats a fluent or consistent revision as correct, or leaves an unresolved discrepancy unmentioned. Revisions can introduce new errors, so every meaningful revision has to be checked against the same task criteria and the source. Sign: 'it reads better' used as the reason to keep a number.

misconceptions.name: Repairs a gap by inventing figures, margins or explanations
misconceptions.description: When the data does not support a claim, asks for an invented margin, a simpler number or a cause (such as discounts) instead of removing or qualifying the claim. Sign: the follow-up adds a new unsupported statement while claiming to fix the old one.

misconceptions.name: Overcorrects by throwing away or restarting everything
misconceptions.description: Discards the whole answer when one claim is wrong, instead of checking that exact claim and keeping the valid work. Targeted repair preserves verified results and the time already spent. Sign: 'delete it all and start again' for a single wrong label.

misconceptions.name: Repairs or judges an answer by surface features, losing evidence or criteria
misconceptions.description: Judges a revision by shortness, tone or polish, or changes its form (a poem, adjectives instead of numbers, removed sections) without checking that required evidence and caveats are still there. A shorter answer that drops a required limitation fails. Sign: word count or style cited as the reason a revision is good.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up the names or meaning of the prompting strategies
misconceptions.description: Confuses zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot and chaining, for example by counting files, reviewers or chatbots instead of worked examples, or by describing adjectives or brand choices as a chain. The strategies differ in what the prompt contains: examples (how many) or linked stages. Sign: a definition that talks about hours, products or file counts.

misconceptions.name: Picks a strategy that does not address the problem observed
misconceptions.description: Reaches for clarification when the problem is formatting, for scheduling when the question is unclear, or for an unrelated step. Each strategy solves a particular kind of problem: examples for a hard-to-describe pattern, clarification for ambiguity, chaining for staged checks. Sign: the chosen technique would not change the defect you described.

misconceptions.name: Treats an explanation, confidence or hidden reasoning as proof of correctness
misconceptions.description: Believes a persuasive method story, a statement of confidence or access to the model's 'private reasoning' shows that a number is right. A concise, checkable method (columns, aggregation, input totals) helps you reproduce the calculation; it does not certify it. Sign: asking for more elaborate reasoning instead of checkable figures.

misconceptions.name: Chains or orders stages without a verification step between them
misconceptions.description: Lets errors flow forward by styling before calculating, interpreting before verifying, or committing to a conclusion before the evidence has been checked. A chain is useful because of the checkpoints between its stages. Sign: the plan goes straight from extraction to recommendation.

misconceptions.name: Guesses or invents when the question or data is ambiguous or missing
misconceptions.description: Continues with an invented decision, treats region labels, filenames or IDs as dates, lets the system invent targets, or charts without context instead of asking a clarifying question or saying the data is not there. Sign: a monthly, profit or target analysis is attempted on a file that has none of those.

misconceptions.name: Treats made-up numbers in an example as data
misconceptions.description: Uses fictional figures in a worked example (for instance a profit figure) as if they could teach the style or fill the file. Examples should be marked format-only and may not carry false facts. Sign: example values appear in the answer.

misconceptions.name: Adds examples, steps or length by default, or because it looks rigorous
misconceptions.description: Assumes more techniques are always better: five examples by default, ten chained prompts, longer prompts, an impressive result or a colourful interface. The right choice depends on whether the task needs examples, clarification or intermediate checks. Sign: the reason given is how the plan looks, not what the task needs.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up the order of the five-step cycle
misconceptions.description: You treat the stages as interchangeable, for example redefining the objective or rewriting constraints right after the tool answers. Each stage uses the output of the one before, and the first check against the source belongs before anything is published or refined. Sign: you jump from "the tool answered" straight to another action.

misconceptions.name: Reads or asks for more than the CSV can support
misconceptions.description: You infer profit, demand, efficiency, growth or causes from totals of net sales, or you ask for forecasts, visits or monthly figures the file does not contain. The CSV has regions, categories and sales amounts for 200 undated transactions, nothing more. Sign: your claim needs a column you cannot point to.

misconceptions.name: Accepts a scale that distorts bar lengths
misconceptions.description: You think the axis is a free design choice: truncating it, hiding its labels or scaling each bar separately seems harmless. Bars encode value by length, so only a shared zero baseline keeps lengths proportional to values. Sign: small differences look large, or readers cannot tell what the axis shows.

misconceptions.name: Accepts a chart or prompt because it looks polished
misconceptions.description: You treat appearance (colours, fonts, animation, a striking look) as a sign that the numbers and claims are right. Looks tell you nothing about whether the measure, totals, labels and statements are correct. Sign: you praise the design before recalculating anything.

misconceptions.name: Assumes the tool did something it did not do
misconceptions.description: You write as if every chatbot can open files and draw charts, or you accept coordinates, descriptions or an "unseen chart" as if they had been produced. A capability counts only when you can see the output and its source. Sign: you cannot say how the chart was made.

misconceptions.name: Treats one problem as proof that everything is right or wrong
misconceptions.description: You react to a single issue by deleting everything, doubting every number, or you accept everything because one part is correct. Totals, chart and narrative can be judged separately: keep what passes its check and repair what fails. Sign: your fix is "start over" or "publish as is".

misconceptions.name: Discards the prompts, outputs and checks
misconceptions.description: You keep only the final picture, or you rename or delete earlier versions once the chart is finished. Without both prompts, both outputs and the check results nobody, including you, can see what changed or reproduce the totals. Sign: you cannot show what V1 looked like.

misconceptions.name: Trusts an AI-drafted prompt or plan without reviewing it
misconceptions.description: You treat a generated prompt as a finished, validated specification, publish it unread or remove the human checks from the workflow. A draft can change your objective, add invented facts or skip verification, and nothing in it guarantees a better result. Sign: you test or run the plan without reading it first.

misconceptions.name: Treats a longer or more elaborate prompt as a better prompt
misconceptions.description: You assume more text, more constraints, a persona or a more complex workflow means a stronger result, or you try to fix a problem by adding words. Quality is shown by what the tested output achieves against the criteria, not by how the prompt sounds. Sign: you prefer a version because it is longer or more complex.

misconceptions.name: Misreads what a fair prompt comparison is for
misconceptions.description: You treat the comparison as a way to make a favoured version win, to rank products or to prove a universal rule such as "AI always wins". A fair comparison holds task, data and criteria constant so you can say what happened in these runs. Sign: your conclusion is wider than your evidence, or the design favours one version.

misconceptions.name: Fills gaps in the task with invented facts
misconceptions.description: When a requirement cannot be met from the file or brief, you supply a guess: a target, a report date, a scenario in place of the data, or you relabel columns. Invented context makes the output look complete while quietly changing the task. Sign: the briefing mentions something nobody told the AI.

misconceptions.name: Lets the task specification drift from the brief
misconceptions.description: You accept or write requirements that differ from the brief: extra deliverables, forecasts the file cannot support, optional outputs, or a changed unit of analysis. The prompt should mirror the brief so the result can be checked against it. Sign: the output list or the grouping no longer matches what the manager asked for.

misconceptions.name: Blends rubric criteria instead of scoring each separately
misconceptions.description: You let one strong criterion lift or sink the others: accurate figures excuse missing limitations, or a missing caveat is waved away as style. Each criterion measures something different and is scored on its own evidence. Sign: your scores for all criteria rise and fall together.

misconceptions.name: Does not keep a labelled trail of versions and results
misconceptions.description: You keep only the final text, give versions the same name or delete weak outputs and scores once you have a winner. Without the draft, your edits and the tested results, nobody can tell what changed or whether the comparison was fair. Sign: you cannot say which edit improved which weakness.

misconceptions.name: Picks one-off, sensitive or unsupported tasks for reuse
misconceptions.description: You choose tasks to save as templates because they feel important, not because they repeat. Reuse pays off when work recurs with a stable structure. A one-time sensitive request, a unique message or an undocumented guess has nothing to template. Sign: the task cannot be described by fixed steps and replaceable inputs.

misconceptions.name: Reuses old inputs, outputs or unresolved placeholders
misconceptions.description: You treat reuse as copying: keeping the first file, last month's values, an earlier output as new data, or leaving brackets in the text. A reusable template separates stable instructions from variable inputs and fills every placeholder from the current run. Sign: this run's report contains something from the last one.

misconceptions.name: Fills a missing or changed input without telling anyone
misconceptions.description: When a source file is missing or its structure changes you carry on anyway: omitting the date, reusing older numbers, inventing a source or hiding the change. The result looks complete but rests on something false or stale. Sign: nobody is told that an input is missing or different.

misconceptions.name: Credits a skill or schedule with powers it does not have
misconceptions.description: You expect a skill or automation to supply new data, approve reports, fix facts such as exchange rates or guarantee accuracy, or you assume or pretend that a feature exists. They only run what you have defined, with the access you have actually set up. Sign: you cannot say where the input comes from or who approves the result.

misconceptions.name: Gives automation access, credentials or authority it should not have
misconceptions.description: You remove human approval, grant broad folder access, allow permanent publishing rights or put passwords and tokens inside a packaged workflow. Automation drafts; people approve and distribute. Sign: nobody reviews before something leaves the team, or the workflow holds secrets.

misconceptions.name: Assumes a reporting period without trusted metadata
misconceptions.description: You treat an undated file as if it supported month-by-month statements, taking the period from a filename, a year or an assumption. Monthly claims need dated records and documented coverage. Sign: your report says "monthly" or "trend" but you cannot point to a date field or period metadata.

misconceptions.name: Keeps too little to reproduce the run
misconceptions.description: You rely on a chart image, a screenshot, a promise to remember or a set of unlabelled chats. Reproducing a result needs the instructions, the input version and the checks that were made. Sign: another person could not repeat your run.

misconceptions.name: Turns a recorded pattern into a cause or a verdict on demand
misconceptions.description: You read East's low count or total as proof of weak demand, a failed promotion or some other mechanism. A pattern in one file shows what was recorded, not why; causes need extra evidence such as store, date or experiment data. A warning sign is a word like "because", "caused" or "proves" next to a count.

misconceptions.name: Treats net sales or transaction value as profit or profitability
misconceptions.description: You move from net sales or value per transaction to margin, profit or return on investment. The CSV has no costs, so none of these can be computed or forecast from it. A warning sign is "profitable", "margin" or "ROI" in a conclusion drawn only from sales columns.

misconceptions.name: Relies on a grouping or measure the CSV cannot support
misconceptions.description: You accept a measure that needs stores, months, operating days or repeat customers. The file has 13 columns and none of these, and they cannot be recovered from row counts. A warning sign is an answer about store productivity or monthly trends from a file with no store ID or date.

misconceptions.name: Accepts, adjusts or explains away a figure without reconciling it to the file
misconceptions.description: You take an AI figure at face value, round it, or bend another number to make it fit instead of recomputing from the CSV. The file is the benchmark, and a mismatch is a prompt to find the cause. A warning sign is a total you cannot trace to a pivot or a formula.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up which measure, field or rank answers the question
misconceptions.description: You choose the wrong field, ratio or end of a ranking, for instance reading the highest region as the lowest, or confusing a count with a value. Each measure answers one question, so check what is being divided by what. A warning sign is an answer that does not use the figure the question names.

misconceptions.name: Jumps to a management action before checking whether the data are comparable
misconceptions.description: You answer a pattern with a target, a closure or a campaign. Before any action, you must know whether the recorded counts are comparable across regions. A warning sign is an action verb (raise, close, promote) appearing before the words coverage or comparable.

misconceptions.name: Treats a plausible explanation as established, or chooses between explanations by how convincing they sound
misconceptions.description: You present a hypothesis such as fewer stores as if it were checked, or settle between two explanations by tone or by averaging them. Competing explanations stay labelled hypotheses until data separates them. A warning sign is the absence of a stated check for each explanation.

misconceptions.name: Judges options by style, length or labels instead of by evidence
misconceptions.description: You pick or rank an option because it is longer, more enthusiastic, better formatted or uses more technical names. These features describe the writing, not the option. A warning sign is a reason that would still be true if the option were wrong.

misconceptions.name: Presents an option's effect as guaranteed, proven or settled
misconceptions.description: You accept a promise of success, a guaranteed financial effect or a claim that other options are useless. The CSV holds historical records with no experiment, so it cannot establish what any future action will do. A warning sign is certain language such as "will", "proven" or "guaranteed" about an action.

misconceptions.name: Assumes East's low count means weak demand, or acts on it before checking coverage
misconceptions.description: You read fewer recorded transactions as fewer customers, or you move straight to price changes or promotions. Counts depend on the stores and the period the extract covers, which the file does not show. A warning sign is an action chosen before the words store list or reporting period appear.

misconceptions.name: Fills an evidence gap with made-up or inferred numbers
misconceptions.description: You supply a baseline, a date or a visit count that the file does not contain, or try to derive it from something else such as transaction IDs. An invented number makes an option look testable when it is not. A warning sign is a figure with no cell in the CSV behind it.

misconceptions.name: Settles a choice, or "challenges" an option, without testing its assumptions
misconceptions.description: You use challenge to add certainty, to drop checked findings, to ignore a data gap, or you settle a conflict by blending options or hiding it. A challenge should expose what would have to be true and what evidence is missing. A warning sign is a conflict resolved without comparing assumptions.

misconceptions.name: Lets the AI approve, rank or choose instead of a person
misconceptions.description: You treat an AI ranking, or an automatic approval of spending, as the decision. The AI can recommend and justify; the manager or named decision owner chooses and is accountable. A warning sign is a plan that starts without a recorded human choice.

misconceptions.name: Lets an AI, a model or a template own or approve the decision
misconceptions.description: You treat the chatbot, a calculation or a saved workflow as the party that approves an action. These tools draft, compute and repeat; they are not accountable. A warning sign is a plan that goes ahead, or publishes, with no named person approving it.

misconceptions.name: Puts the human pause at the wrong point in the workflow
misconceptions.description: You place the pause before the task is defined, at an irrelevant event, or after the plan is already published. The pause belongs after the options are compared and challenged and before planning begins. A warning sign is a step that produces a plan before anyone has chosen a direction.

misconceptions.name: Treats style, length, persona or raw volume as what makes a plan or brief useful
misconceptions.description: You add praise, a more elaborate role prompt, a longer description or the whole chat log to a plan. None of these says who does what or what the evidence is. A warning sign is an addition that would still be there if the plan were unusable.

misconceptions.name: Asserts an outcome, benchmark, cause or measure the file cannot support
misconceptions.description: You write an uplift, a profit rise, a testimonial, a benchmark or a causal verdict into a plan or recommendation. The CSV has no baseline, costs, experiment or store and date fields to support them. A warning sign is a number or a cause with no cell in the CSV behind it.

misconceptions.name: Defines success vaguely or as something that cannot be checked
misconceptions.description: You describe the end of an action as an unlabelled chart, a changed goal or a feeling. A success measure should be observable and tied to the action's aim, such as confirmed comparable coverage. A warning sign is a measure nobody could tick off as done or not done.

misconceptions.name: Reuses a chain or earlier results on new data without recalculating
misconceptions.description: You copy the East numbers, recommendations or assumptions into a run for another region or file. Instructions can be reused, but inputs and conclusions are specific to the data. A warning sign is a figure that appears in the new brief without a new calculation behind it.

misconceptions.name: Pushes ahead while a figure is unchecked or a limitation is hidden
misconceptions.description: You approve, publish or rely on a recommendation although a number has not been verified, or you leave out the data limitations. An unchecked figure can change the recommended action. A warning sign is a clear narrative that nobody has traced back to the CSV.

misconceptions.name: Judges a claim by its wording or surroundings instead of its evidence
misconceptions.description: Accepts or tries to fix a claim by making it sound more confident, adding decoration, or by confusing the claim with the tools and checks used to examine it. A claim is supported only by a source column, a calculation or a document that really exists. A sign of this error is polishing a statement rather than asking where it comes from.

misconceptions.name: Treats a gap between regional totals as proof of a cause, bias or customer quality
misconceptions.description: Reads a lower regional total as evidence of weaker customers, weaker demand or unfair treatment. Totals show that two numbers differ, not why, and a claim about bias or customer value needs variables that measure it. A sign is that the explanation contains a word such as because, unfair or less valuable that no column supports.

misconceptions.name: Shares more personal data than the task needs
misconceptions.description: Treats a file being available, or looking complete, as a reason to upload or paste all of it, names and contact details included. Data minimisation means preparing a copy with only the fields the task uses, and doing it before sharing. A sign is an upload plan that starts from the whole export instead of from the question.

misconceptions.name: Chooses where to upload by speed or appearance instead of approval
misconceptions.description: Decides whether to use an AI tool because it is fast, popular or looks modern. None of these says whether the account and service are approved for the data or how it is shared, kept and used. A sign is that the checklist for the upload mentions the tool's features but not permission or data sensitivity.

misconceptions.name: Lets instructions inside a document or web page direct the work
misconceptions.description: Treats a sentence found in uploaded or retrieved content as if the user or a manager had said it, because it is phrased as an order or looks official. Content is data to analyse; only the user's request and the permissions set decide what the AI may do. A sign is that the plan involves sending, revealing or forwarding something because the document said so.

misconceptions.name: Lets a connected tool act with broad, standing or unreviewed access
misconceptions.description: Grants a tool more permission than the task needs, keeps it after the task, trusts its choice of recipient or skips the human check before an external action. External actions such as sending a report are hard to undo. A sign is that nobody can say who approved the step or what the tool could reach.

misconceptions.name: Believes a line in the prompt is enough to stop a harmful action
misconceptions.description: Assumes that telling the model to ignore hostile instructions fully protects a workflow where the tool can send email or change files. A prompt states a boundary but does not remove the capability. Protection also needs minimal permissions, account controls and human approval.

misconceptions.name: Treats surface details as the record instead of the data, method and approvals
misconceptions.description: Counts titles, logos, colours, length, screenshots or a model's name as documentation, or looks to them to explain a numeric difference. None of these lets a colleague repeat the work. A sign is a record that could be identical whether the result were right or wrong.

misconceptions.name: Expects tidy files, labels or structure to replace checking
misconceptions.description: Assumes that organising files, or labelling claims as findings, assumptions and next actions, verifies them or approves them. Structure only shows where things are and which statements are evidence. A sign is skipping the recomputation because the report looks well organised.

misconceptions.name: Offers assurance, emphasis or repetition where evidence is needed
misconceptions.description: Treats a confident statement, a promise, a longer restatement, a highlight or another copy of a chart as making a claim traceable. Traceability means a reader can follow the claim to the data, table and method behind it. A sign is that nothing in the handover could be recomputed.

misconceptions.name: Records a method that does not compute the quantity being reported
misconceptions.description: Writes a method note whose grouping, aggregation or column does not produce the stated figure, such as sorting or counting columns when the report gives net sales by region. A sufficient note names the filter or grouping and the exact column and operation. A sign is that following the note literally would give a different number.

misconceptions.name: Leaves chats and inputs unlabelled, unversioned or mixed together
misconceptions.description: Organises related chats by giving them vague or identical titles, keeping inputs only in the latest reply, or mixing unrelated files into every thread. A colleague then cannot tell what each thread holds or which file version it used. A sign is a thread you can only find by remembering when you wrote it.

misconceptions.name: Settles a disagreement between two results without tracing their source
misconceptions.description: Resolves two different totals by choosing the bigger one, accepting more decimals or deciding both support the claim. A difference means the inputs, filters or formulas differ, and files can share a name while differing in content or version. A sign is a decision reached without opening either file.

misconceptions.name: Expects reproducibility to mean identical AI wording
misconceptions.description: Judges whether a result reproduced by whether the AI's prose matches word for word. AI wording can vary even when data and request are unchanged. A reproduction check is about the data, the method and whether the key figures agree at the stated precision.

misconceptions.name: Treats a polished AI output as evidence that it is correct
misconceptions.description: Assumes that precise decimals, fluent prose or a tidy chart mean the figures were calculated and are right. Such output can be generated without any calculation behind it. The warning sign is accepting a result because it looks finished, with no independent recomputation.

misconceptions.name: Lets the AI verify or approve its own work
misconceptions.description: Asks the model whether it is right, or lets it confirm, decide or act on its own result. Self-assurance is more generated text, not an independent check. The sign is a workflow with no human comparison against the source and no human approval before an action.

misconceptions.name: Treats a recorded total or count as proof of a cause
misconceptions.description: Moves from what the file records to why it happens, for example weak demand, poor store performance or the effect of a promotion. A total or count cannot show that. The sign is a causal or performance claim with no data about stores, dates or customers behind it.

misconceptions.name: Mixes up totals, counts, averages and gross versus net
misconceptions.description: Confuses what a figure measures: a total with a per-transaction value, gross with net, or a weighted figure with an average of averages. The conclusion then points the wrong way. The sign is a statement with no formula (sum, count, sum divided by count) that you can recompute.

misconceptions.name: Relies on data the file does not contain
misconceptions.description: Asks for or assumes dates, currency, costs, profit, targets, store identifiers or unique customers, none of which the CSV holds. The result is a trend, margin, dollar value or per-store claim that has to be invented. The sign is a request that the available fields cannot support.

misconceptions.name: Accepts a long or vague instruction as a substitute for a testable one
misconceptions.description: Believes that length, a grand role, "be careful" or "try again" improves a prompt, brief or plan. None of these names a field, an output, an owner or a check, so nothing can be tested. The sign is a request with many words and no observable success criterion.

misconceptions.name: Gives the AI more data or more access than the task needs
misconceptions.description: Shares unneeded personal or sensitive fields, follows instructions that appear inside files as if they were commands, or grants broad access and automatic sending. Each increases harm if something goes wrong. The sign is full uploads, full permissions or no human approval step.

misconceptions.name: Reuses or hands over AI work without a reproducible record
misconceptions.description: Keeps only the final output, or reruns a saved template without re-checking the new input. Nobody else can then verify or repeat the result. The sign is a handover with no file version, prompt text, method note or recorded checks.

feedbackTemplates.body: Look at what you actually gave the tool. A filename, a cover image or an unrelated document does not contain the values the task depends on. Ask what the answer will be built from, then provide that: the real file, a data extract or a verified summary. If the evidence is not in the chat, the reply cannot be based on it.

A file you have not attached, or a tool that cannot open it, gives you no analysis, only text that sounds like one. Check for the attach control or ask the tool what it can read. If it cannot read the file, calculate in a spreadsheet and paste a small verified extract, saying where it came from. Never accept a total you cannot trace back to the data.

Start from the question and the reader. A comparison of exact values is shown best in a table; a pattern across categories in a chart; an idea in text. Ask which format lets the reader see the answer at once and lets you check it. Then request that format, and a chart specification if the tool cannot draw one.

Ask who will answer for this decision if it goes wrong. A chatbot, a template or a chart tool cannot. It is the responsible manager or learner who defines the task, verifies the numbers, interprets the limits and approves. Use AI for drafts and keep the sign-off, with your own check, for a person.

Appearance can be generated; understanding has to be shown. The best test is whether someone can reproduce a calculation, explain a chart in their own words and say how a result was checked. When you judge your own AI-assisted work, do that test before you trust how it looks.

Ask what the step is for, not what it looks like. Setting the task and success criteria is Define; writing the request is Design; running it is Execute; checking the result against the task and evidence is Evaluate; changing the request because of what the check showed is Refine. Put the step after the check or before the run to see where it belongs.

In this course a token is a unit of text that the model processes. It is not a number in your table, an axis on a chart, an approval, or a stored record. That is why the model can produce text that looks right without having checked a fact. Keep the idea simple: text in, text out, and your job is to check what it says.

First decide what kind of problem you have. Layout and ordering problems are about how real information is shown. An invented citation, number or fact is a problem with the evidence itself. Use the match: invented source, check the source; wrong sum, recalculate; wrong label, check the column; unsupported cause, qualify it.

Look at the verbs. A comparison can show that one region is lower than another; it cannot show why. Keep the verified number, and relabel the reason as an untested hypothesis. Then say what evidence would test it, such as targets, a time series, store coverage or a demand measure.

When the file lacks something, the honest move is to say so. Do not substitute a different guess (stores, profit, dates), and do not ask the AI to invent the gap. List what is missing, state that the claim cannot be made from this file, and ask for the extra evidence or change the question.

A check is only a check if it does not depend on the thing being checked. Use something else: open the source, recalculate in a spreadsheet, or have a person review the evidence. The AI can help to list assumptions or find what to check, but the judgement about whether the evidence supports the claim stays with you.

Distrust a claim, not a format. A long answer or a table can be right, and a chart can show data well. Check each claim against its evidence, keep what is verified, qualify what is only partly supported and remove what is unsupported. A rule that rejects everything is as unhelpful as one that accepts everything.

Credibility cues are cheap to produce and easy to fake. Open the source and check the title and the passage; recalculate the number from the data; and ask whether the evidence actually reached the tool. If you cannot verify a source, remove the claim that depends on it.

Ask first: what decision does the manager face? The question and the evidence follow from that, and the format follows from the reader. Presentation choices are easy to change later, but an unclear problem will make every later step weak. Write the decision down before you open the chatbot.

List what the file contains and what it lacks, then compare it with the question. Profit needs costs, a missed target needs targets, and a trend needs dates. If a column is missing, change the question to one the data can answer, or obtain the data. Do not ask AI to estimate it.

A success criterion must be something you can check against the result: every region appears once, the totals match the source, the measure is named, no currency is invented. Rewrite each vague wish as an observable test. If you cannot say how you would check it, it is not yet a criterion.

Ask what the task cannot be done without. Is it the audience, the decision, the input data or a column such as dates? Supply that item directly. Extra length, background or synonyms may make the request longer, but the missing requirement is still missing.

Whenever a word like "best" appears, ask: best by which measure? Name the metric (for example the sum of Net_Sales_Amount per region) and check that the data contains it. If two metrics matter, write two separate questions.

Start from the decision, not the dataset. Two managers can use the same file and still need different questions, outputs and checks. Write the context and the success criteria separately for each decision, and do not let the tool decide the objective for you.

A prompt needs a named measure, a grouping and an output you can check. Look at your prompt: could someone else tell which column to sum and by which column to group? If not, add the exact field names and the shape of the result. Tone and breadth words do not tell the chatbot what to calculate.

A role changes voice, not accuracy: it cannot give the model the data or make a number right. Ask what the sentence lets you observe or check in the answer. Spend the words on the measure, the grouping, the output format and the limits, and verify the figures independently.

Length is not quality. Extra personas, headings or examples can introduce conflicts or false assumptions. For each sentence ask: if I delete it, what changes in the answer? Keep what improves a result you can test, and compare two versions on the same rubric before deciding.

Examples show a pattern; they are not records. If the CSV or a verified table is not in the conversation, the model has no source rows, so any totals would be invented. Attach the file or paste the table, or say clearly that the data is not available, before polishing anything else.

Sort each sentence by the job it does: what to do (instruction), who it is for (context), what to use (input), what shape to return (output), what to avoid or include (constraint). A column that exists in the file is data; a limit on what you may claim is a constraint. Re-label your prompt line by line to check.

If the file does not contain something, the prompt must not assume it. Check the field list: no currency, no costs, no dates. Ask for the unit to stay unspecified, and do not substitute another measure or an estimate. A plausible guess is still an unsupported claim.

The provider layouts group the same needs under different names, so none is compulsory. When two prompts hold the same task, data and limits, do not rank them by look or length: run both, score the outputs against one rubric and keep the one that does the job.

A follow-up is a further instruction that uses the conversation you already have to ask for one change. It does not check the data for you. Whenever a follow-up changes anything, you still compare the new answer with the source. Ask: what does this message change, and how will I check it?

A follow-up works when it names what is wrong and what you want instead, and says what must stay fixed. Look at yours: could a colleague tell which defect you meant and how you would know it is fixed? If not, rewrite it as 'defect + desired change + keep unchanged'.

Add context only if it changes the answer: audience, purpose, time available, length. Ask of every detail you add: would the answer or the decision be different without it? If not, leave it out, and do not remove the business question the answer is supposed to serve.

A revision can fix one thing and break another, and a smooth narrative is not evidence. After each follow-up, compare the new answer with the same criteria as before: right measure, all regions, totals reconcile, caveat still visible. If a checked number changed, restore it and say so.

A claim the data cannot support is repaired by removing or qualifying it, not by adding another unsupported figure or cause. Check what the file actually contains (no costs, no currency, no dates) and ask the chatbot to correct the wording while keeping the verified totals.

When one claim is wrong, check and correct that exact claim and keep everything valid. Deleting the whole answer throws away verified work and gives you nothing to compare against. Name the specific problem in the next prompt and ask for a revised answer.

Do not judge a revision by length, tone or polish. Check it against all the task criteria: the right measure, all regions, evidence still present, required limitations still visible. A shorter answer that drops a caveat or a number has failed the completeness check, however neat it looks.

Name the strategies by what the prompt contains: zero-shot has no worked example, one-shot has one, few-shot has several, chaining links separate prompts through checked outputs. Counts of files, reviewers or chatbots are different dimensions. Re-read the definition and match it to what you would see in the prompt.

Start from the problem, then choose the strategy. A format that is wrong needs an example; an ambiguous question needs a clarification; a multi-stage analysis needs a chain with checks. Ask: would this technique actually change the defect I observed? If not, pick a different one.

A fluent explanation or a stated confidence is not evidence, and a model's private reasoning is not something you can inspect. Ask instead for a compact, checkable method: the columns used, the aggregation and the input totals. Then recompute them from the CSV or a spreadsheet yourself.

A chain earns its value from the checks between stages. Put the verification (totals reconciled with the file) before interpretation, and do not style or conclude first. Look at your plan and mark where you would stop and check the intermediate output.

When the question is ambiguous or the file lacks what a task needs (dates, costs, targets), do not guess. Ask one focused clarifying question, or request the missing data. Filenames, IDs and region labels are not substitutes for the real field.

An example teaches format or tone; its numbers are not data. Mark examples as format-only, keep them free of false facts, and tell the model that every figure in the answer must come from the file. Fictional profit figures cannot teach style and may be copied.

Do not add techniques because they look rigorous. If a simple request already meets your criteria, keep it and verify. Add examples when the pattern is hard to describe, chaining when you need checks between steps, and clarification when the question is ambiguous. Choose by what the task needs.

Write down what each of the five stages produces and what the next stage needs from it. Then find the point where you first compare the tool's output with the CSV. Anything you publish, refine or redefine before that point rests on an unchecked output.

For each claim or request, name the column in the CSV that would support it. If you cannot, the claim or the request goes beyond the data. A ranking of sums supports a statement about recorded net sales and nothing about profit, demand, efficiency or causes.

Look at the first tick on the value axis. If it is not zero, bar lengths no longer match values; a bar for 70% of the maximum can look tiny. A fair chart for comparing sizes uses one shared zero baseline with labelled units. Hiding the labels hides the problem; it does not fix it.

Set the visuals aside and check three things: do the labels name the right measure, do the totals match your own spreadsheet, and is every sentence supported by a number? A good-looking chart can be wrong and a plain one can be right. Decide on the checks, then on the design.

Ask what evidence shows that the tool read the file and drew the chart: a row count, a table you can recompute, a visible image. If the tool cannot do it, use a spreadsheet or request a specification you can build elsewhere, and state which part came from where.

Split the output into parts (totals, labels, scale, order, commentary) and check each one. Keep the parts that pass, fix the ones that fail, and recheck after the change. Throwing away verified work wastes effort, and publishing unsupported text because the chart is right passes a claim you never tested.

Save every prompt version with its output, the tool and date, the input filename and the checks you made. Label versions honestly and never rename an early draft as final. A peer should be able to repeat your totals from the record without using the AI output.

Read the draft requirement by requirement and compare it with your brief: does each line keep the objective, use only fields in the CSV and leave a place for you to check before the next stage? A draft is a proposal. What makes a plan safe to test is the review points you keep or add, not the confidence of its wording.

Ask what each extra sentence changes that you can check. Then compare the outputs, not the prompts: if a shorter version meets every criterion, the extra length has not earned anything. Match the fix to the defect; a wrong unit or scope is not repaired by more detail.

Write the conclusion you are entitled to: which version did what, on this task, under these conditions. Check that everything except the prompt method was held constant, and that no version was favoured by sequence, effort or origin. A tie supports a statement about this task and nothing broader.

Ask what the file or the manager actually supplies for this requirement. If the answer is nothing, either ask the manager for the real information or remove the requirement. Never fill the gap with a guess; mark it as unknown and state it in the limitations.

Put the brief and the prompt side by side and tick off the outputs, the grouping unit and the data used. Anything in the prompt that is not in the brief, or in the file, is drift; anything missing from the prompt is a gap. A precise brief states exactly what must be produced.

Score one criterion at a time, pointing to the part of the briefing that is your evidence. Accurate numbers earn credit where numbers are scored; a gap elsewhere costs points where that is scored. If you cannot point to evidence for a 2, it is not a 2.

Label each version (A, B as drafted, C with edits marked) and keep its output, settings, time and score together. Keep the unsuccessful runs, since they show what the edits fixed. A reviewer should be able to follow the trail from the first draft to the final briefing.

Ask whether the task recurs, whether its steps stay the same and which parts change each time. Recurring work with a stable structure and variable inputs is a template candidate. Sensitive, unrepeatable or unsupported items are not, and putting them into a saved prompt spreads the problem.

Before each run, list the placeholders and write the current value for each. Check that no earlier file, number or output feeds the new run, and that no bracket is left in the result. If the file structure changed, retest before you reuse the instructions.

Make the workflow check that the source exists and has the expected columns before it calculates. If a check fails, produce an exception report that says what is missing or changed and stop. Never replace the missing item with an invented or older one without saying so.

Write down what the feature really does: which instructions and resources it holds, which inputs it needs and which permissions it has. Anything beyond that is your responsibility. If you do not have the feature, practise with a manual checklist and say so honestly.

Give the workflow the least access it needs: a named source, a named destination and draft-only output. Keep credentials out of saved instructions, and keep a review gate before any distribution or publication.

Check the file for a date or period field and for documentation from a trusted source. If neither exists, do not claim a period or trend; ask for period-labelled data. Formatting, audience lines and placeholder names are not the risk here: unsupported time claims are.

List what a stranger would need to rerun your work: the versioned template, the exact input file and the log of checks. Anything that is only in your memory or in an unlabelled screenshot cannot be audited, so save it with a label.

A count or a total tells you what was recorded, not why. Look for the word that jumps from "East has fewer records" to a reason such as weak demand or a promotion, and ask what evidence in the file could support that reason. Rewrite the claim as an observation plus a labelled hypothesis, and name the data that would test it.

Net sales and value per transaction are revenue figures. Profit, margin and return need costs, and this CSV has none. Before you accept a conclusion about profitability, ask which column holds the cost, and if there is none, restate the claim in terms of net sales only.

Check the 13 columns before accepting a measure. There is no store ID, date, operating-day or customer ID field, so anything that depends on them cannot be built or inferred from row counts. Replace it with a grouping the columns do support, such as region or product category, and list the missing field as a data request.

A figure that does not match the file is a signal to recompute, not to adjust, round or explain away. Rebuild the total with a pivot table, compare it with the AI figure, and find where they differ. Only a reconciled number should go into a table or a diagnosis.

Re-read what the question asks for and name the measure: a count, a total, a value per transaction, or a rank. Then check the formula (for example total net sales divided by the group's own transaction count) and which end of the ranking you need. Reading the table again with that definition in hand usually settles it.

Before acting on a regional pattern, ask whether the recorded counts are comparable: the same stores, the same period, the same extraction rules. The file cannot show this, so the first move is to ask for that information. Write down what you would do if coverage matched and what you would do if it did not.

A plausible reason is still a hypothesis until data separates it from the alternatives. Label each explanation as a hypothesis, write the check that would distinguish it from the others, and never merge two explanations into a single cause or pick one for sounding stronger.

Length, tone and formatting tell you how an option is written, not how good it is. Ask instead what evidence the option needs, how much its answer would change the decision and how hard it is to get. Rank options on those, and ignore which one sounds most polished.

The CSV records what happened; it contains no experiment, so it cannot guarantee what an action will do. Look for words like "will", "proven" or "guaranteed" and replace them with "may" plus the evidence still needed. A good option states what it would test, not what it will deliver.

A low recorded count can come from fewer stores, a shorter reporting window or lower activity, and the file cannot tell you which. Before treating the count as weak demand, ask what store and date coverage each region has. Put the coverage check first and keep any price or promotion idea on hold.

If the file does not hold a number, you cannot create it or derive it from something else, such as visits from transaction IDs. Mark it as an evidence gap and say who could supply it. An option that depends on it stays contingent until the real data arrive.

A challenge should make an option's hidden assumptions visible, not make it sound stronger or remove inconvenient findings. Ask what would have to be true for the option to work and what evidence is missing. When two options conflict, compare their assumptions side by side before choosing.

An AI can propose, rank and justify options, but it cannot approve spending or choose a direction. Name the person who owns the decision and record their choice and reasoning before any plan is written. If you cannot name that person, the plan is not ready.

Decision authority stays with a named person. A chatbot drafts, a spreadsheet computes and a template repeats a process, and none of them is accountable for approving an action. Add a line to the plan naming who approves it and when, and do not let any tool publish or act before that approval.

Put the human pause after the options are compared and challenged and before any planning or action. Check your workflow: is there a step that produces a plan, or sends something, before a person has chosen a direction? If so, move the pause earlier, or split the chain into separate turns.

A plan becomes usable through what it says, not how it sounds: who does it, which inputs they need, what they must deliver and how the outcome will be checked. Remove praise, persona text and bulk material, and ask whether a colleague could carry out the plan from what remains.

If the CSV has no cell behind a number or a cause, it does not belong in a plan as a fact. Look for uplift, benchmarks, profit, testimonials and causal claims, and either delete them or label them as hypotheses to test. State the data you would need to support each.

State success as something observable that you could tick off: for example, comparable store and date coverage confirmed, or the gaps documented. Avoid measures such as an unlabelled chart or a changed goal. Ask whether two reviewers would agree on whether it was met.

A saved chain keeps its instructions, but every input and output belongs to the file it was run on. When you reuse it, swap in the new region or file, recalculate each figure and record the new limitations. Never paste results from the earlier run into the new brief.

Before approving, trace each figure in the recommendation to a cell or a pivot you have seen, and keep the data limitations in the brief. If one calculation is unchecked, hold approval until it is verified, since it could change the action. A clear narrative is not evidence.

A claim is supported only if you can name the column, calculation or document behind it. Confident wording, decoration, or the checking work around a claim says nothing about whether it is true. Ask where the statement comes from; if you cannot say, delete it rather than polish it.

A difference between regional totals shows that the totals differ, not why, and not that anyone was treated unfairly. A claim about bias, customer value or cause needs variables that measure it. Write what the file does show, and list the evidence the explanation would need.

A file being available is not a reason to share all of it. Start from what the task needs and prepare a copy with only those fields, before the upload and not after it. Then open that copy and read every column header before you send it.

Speed, popularity and a modern interface describe the tool, not your permission to use it. Before uploading, check that the account and service are approved for this kind of data, then look at the sharing, retention and data-use settings. If you are unsure, stop and ask first.

Text inside a document or web page is content to analyse; it is never an instruction from you or approval from anyone. Ask who actually authorised the step: only your own request and the permissions you set can. Ignore the embedded sentence, flag it, and continue with the approved task.

Each extra permission is one more thing that can go wrong unnoticed, and an email sent to the wrong person is hard to take back. Grant only what the task needs, keep drafting separate from sending, and put a human check of recipient, content and attachments in front of every external action. Try a small pilot before widening access.

A line in the prompt states what you want, but it cannot stop an action the tool is allowed to take. Pair it with real controls: minimal permissions, draft kept separate from send, and human approval for anything external. Ask yourself what would happen if the model ignored your instruction.

Titles, logos, colours, length, screenshot counts and a model's name are easy to see but do not let anyone repeat your work. Ask what a colleague would need to get the same number: the data version, the final prompts, the method and who approved what. Keep those and ignore the rest.

Tidy files and labels show where things are and which statements are evidence; they verify nothing. A line marked as a hypothesis is still a hypothesis, and a well-organised report still needs its numbers recomputed from the source. Use structure to make checking easier, then do the check.

A claim becomes traceable when a reader can follow it to the data, table and method behind it. Confidence, promises, longer restatements, highlights and extra copies of a chart give them nothing to recompute. Hand over the file version and the steps instead.

A method note is enough only if following it produces the reported figure. Check three things: which rows (the filter), which grouping, and which column is aggregated and how (sum, count or average). Run the note's steps on the file yourself; if you do not get the reported number, the note is not enough.

When several chats and files feed one analysis, a reader must be able to tell what each contains and which version it used. Name chats by purpose, write the file version beside each analysis, and keep unrelated material out. If a thread can only be found by its newest reply, rename it.

Two different totals mean the two analyses differ in file content or version, in filters, or in formulas. More decimals, a higher number or calling both results proof of the same claim does not find which. Compare the files themselves, not their names, and then compare the calculation steps.

Reproducing a result means repeating the data, the method and the numbers. AI wording can vary even when the data and the request are unchanged, so word-for-word agreement is the wrong test. Compare the key figures at the stated precision and treat differences in prose as normal.

You treated a polished output as if it were evidence. Neat tables, figures to the cent, confident prose and tidy charts can all be produced without any calculation behind them. Before you accept a result, recompute the key figure in a spreadsheet and compare it with the AI's version.

You let the AI vouch for itself. Asking a model whether it is right, or letting it approve its own result or action, gives you more generated text, not an independent check. Put a human check between the AI and anything that matters: a spreadsheet total, a reviewer's sign-off, a named approver.

You moved from what the file records to why it happens. A total or a count is a fact about recorded transactions. Reasons such as weak demand, store performance or the effect of an action need data the file does not hold. Label the claim as a hypothesis and list the data that would test it.

Check which measure the statement is about. A total, a count and a per-transaction average answer different questions, and gross, net or an average of averages is not the same as the overall net figure. Write the formula for each number (sum, count, sum divided by count) and recompute it from the file.

You relied on something the file does not contain. The CSV has no dates, currency, costs, profit, targets, store identifiers or unique customers, so any trend, margin, dollar value or per-store claim would have to be invented. Reread what the fields actually provide and ask for the missing data instead of filling the gap.

You accepted a specification that sounds thorough but cannot be checked. Length, a grand role or "try again" does not say which field, output, owner or test of success you want. Name the exact fields, the output format, the checks and what must not be assumed, and change only the part that failed.

You gave the AI more data or more power than the task needs. Share only the fields the task requires, use an approved tool, and treat instructions found inside files or web pages as untrusted content, never as commands. Grant the lowest access that works and keep sending or publishing as a human action.

A result that nobody else can reproduce is hard to trust. Keep the unaltered file (name and version), the exact prompts, the method (filter, field, formula), the checks you ran, and the tool and date. Rerun a saved template only after re-checking that the new input has the same structure.

lessons.body:
This page restates the official course syllabus (Faculty of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, National Economics University; revised 12 November 2026). Anything the syllabus itself marks "to be confirmed" is shown here as **not yet specified**. Nothing has been filled in on its behalf.

## General information

## Faculty and lecturers

Faculty: Faculty of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence.

| Assoc. Prof. Dr. Ha Minh Hoang | hoanghm@neu.edu.vn |

| MSc. Ngo Thai Hoa | hoatn@neu.edu.vn |

## Course description

This introductory micro-credential develops practical skills for working with generative AI in academic and business tasks. You use chatbots, define a task and its success criteria, design prompts, improve responses through follow-ups, select prompting strategies and evaluate AI-assisted results.

You practise data visualisation, AI-assisted prompt planning, reusable workflows and evidence-based business decisions using a retail CSV. Two connected retail cases are used: a regional sales visualisation and a business investigation that leads to an action plan. You verify calculations and claims and apply privacy, security and documentation practices.

### Main content

1. AI chatbots, limitations and task definition (Periods 1–3)
2. Prompt anatomy, follow-up prompts and strategies (Periods 4–6)
3. Task execution, AI-assisted prompting and workflow reuse (Periods 7–9)
4. Evidence-based retail problem solving (Periods 10–12)
5. Privacy, security, documentation and reproducibility (Periods 13–14)

The instructional cycle that runs through every module is **Define → Design → Execute → Evaluate → Refine**.
