lessons.title: Course Overview
lessons.description: What the course teaches, the five-stage cycle, the five modules, the retail CSV and what it cannot show, how to study each period, and the rules for checking figures and protecting data.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this page you can:
objectives: Describe the cycle Define → Design → Execute → Evaluate → Refine and what you do at each stage
Name the five modules and the periods each one covers
List what the retail CSV contains and, more importantly, what it does not contain
Follow the study routine for every period: read, predict, quiz with confidence, review flashcards
State the verification and privacy rules you will apply from Period 1
lessons.body:
Generative AI can produce a fluent answer to almost any request. This course teaches the harder skill: getting an answer you can actually use in a study or business decision, and noticing when you cannot. You will do that on one retail data set, with a spreadsheet beside the chatbot, and you will check every figure before you rely on it. No programming is needed.

> [!ghi-nho] A polished answer is not a checked answer. Across all 14 periods you ask the same question of every AI output: what did the tool actually do, and how do I know the result is right?

## What you learn

| You learn to | Where it shows |
|---|---|
| Recognise suitable chatbot tasks, their limitations and their risks | Periods 1–3 and 13 |
| Define a task, then design, run, evaluate and refine prompts | Periods 3–9 |
| Turn AI output into reliable analysis, decisions and reusable, documented workflows | Periods 7–14 |

## The cycle: Define → Design → Execute → Evaluate → Refine

Every activity follows the same five stages. The retail example shows what each one looks like.

| Stage | The question you ask | Example in the retail case |
|---|---|---|
| **Define** | Which decision, which data, which output, and how will I know the answer is right? | The manager wants to know which region contributes the most net sales; you need a table, a chart and a short, evidence-based reading |
| **Design** | How do I write the prompt (instruction, context, input, output, constraints) and which strategy fits? | Name the fields Store_Region and Net_Sales_Amount, ask for a four-row table, say the currency is unspecified |
| **Execute** | Did the tool really read the file? What did it return? | Run the prompt; record the tool, the date and whether the file was opened or you supplied a table |
| **Evaluate** | Do the totals, labels, scale and claims match the source? | Rebuild the four sums in a spreadsheet and compare them one by one |
| **Refine** | What one targeted change improves the result without breaking what was already correct? | Sort the bars, regenerate, then check that the figures did not change |

> [!canh-bao] Evaluate is not optional. A response that skips it can look excellent and still be wrong. The cycle only counts as finished when a human has compared the result with the source.

## Five modules, 14 periods

| Module | Periods | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 1. AI Chatbots and Task Definition | 1–3 | Choose inputs, tools and output formats; understand what a language model can and cannot do; write a four-part task brief |
| 2. Design: Prompts and Prompting Strategies | 4–6 | Build a five-function prompt; improve answers with follow-ups; choose zero-shot, few-shot, explanation, chaining or clarification |
| 3. Execute: Apply, Compare and Automate | 7–9 | Run the regional chart case; compare human-written, AI-drafted and human-edited prompts; prepare a reusable template and a reviewed scheduling plan |
| 4. Prompting for Data-Driven Problem Solving | 10–12 | Diagnose, compare options and build an action plan with human review and success measures |
| 5. Privacy, Security, Documentation and Reproducibility | 13–14 | Protect sensitive inputs, handle untrusted content, control AI permissions, save a working record and reproduce a result |

Each module opens with a short materials page that says which attached file covers which period. The course ends with an integrated final assessment that mixes all five modules.

## The two retail cases and the CSV

Both cases use the same file: **Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv**, with 200 transactions (one row each) and 13 columns.

| Fields | What they hold |
|---|---|
| Transaction_ID | One identifier per transaction |
| Store_Region, Product_Category | Four regions and four product categories |
| Payment_Method, Customer_Type | The payment method and the kind of customer for each transaction |
| Unit_Price, Items_Sold | Price and quantity |
| Gross_Amount, Discount_Percent, Discount_Amount, Net_Sales_Amount | The amount before discount, the discount and the amount after it |
| Average_Price_Per_Item, Effective_Discount_Per_Item | Per-item figures derived from the amounts above |

- **Case 1 (Period 7):** which region contributes the most net sales? You produce a four-region table and a bar chart, check them, and improve the chart.
- **Case 2 (Periods 10–12, with handover in 13–14):** a business investigation of the East region that ends in an evidence-based action plan.

The file has **no** transaction dates, no currency, no costs, no store identifiers or store counts, no operating days, no targets and no profit. That is deliberate: much of the course is about not claiming what the data cannot show.

> [!canh-bao] The file is provided for teaching and its real-world origin is not established. Use it to practise method. Do not treat its figures as facts about a real retailer.

:::Predict before you read: which of these questions can the CSV answer?
Decide for each one, then open the next block.

1. Which region has the highest total net sales?
2. In which month were sales highest?
3. Which payment method brings in the most net sales?
4. Which region is the most profitable?
5. How many Electronics transactions were recorded in East?
:::

:::Check your prediction
Questions 1, 3 and 5 can be answered by grouping and counting the recorded rows. Question 2 cannot: there are no dates. Question 4 cannot: there are no costs or profit figures. Spotting which requests the file can support is the first skill in the course.
:::

## How to study each period

1. **Read** the lesson. Pages open with a retail situation and end with a short "check it yourself" step that points you at the CSV or a spreadsheet.
2. **Predict** before you read: where a page has a "Predict before you read" or "Find the error" block, commit to an answer first, then open it.
3. **Quiz** with confidence: before you see whether an answer is right, rate how sure you are. A wrong answer tells you which misconception it matches and what to try next.
4. **Review** the flashcards the next day, then a week later.

Each period page is designed for about 45 minutes. The lecture notes and slides give more detail; use them alongside the lesson, not instead of it.

## Assessment and practice

The syllabus lists 14 formative checkpoints (one multiple-choice question per period, ungraded), three applied activities and a final assessment. The quiz in each period is a longer practice set for that checkpoint. Weights and pass criteria for the activities and the final assessment are not yet specified in the syllabus, so nothing here assumes them.

| Activity | Period | Task | Practice time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. AI-assisted retail data visualisation | 7 | Case 1: regional chart, independent check and one design revision | 55–70 minutes |
| 2. Human vs AI-assisted prompt design (A/B/C) | 8 | Compare three versions of a one-page briefing with one five-criterion rubric | 70–90 minutes |
| 3. Evidence-based retail decision making | 10–12 | Case 2: diagnosis, options and action plan, with a handover folder | 100–130 minutes |

These times are practice estimates and do not change the 14 teaching periods. Each activity sheet carries a 10-point practice rubric that is formative unless a course assessor approves a weight.

## Rules for working with figures

1. **Check before you accept.** Recompute every number you plan to use, for example with a pivot table or SUMIF, and compare it with the AI's version.
2. **Label what you write.** Separate verified fact, interpretation, hypothesis and data needed.
3. **Do not invent what is missing.** Never add a currency, profit, trend or cause that the file does not contain.
4. **Report what the tool really did.** If the chatbot could not open the file or draw a chart, say so and use your spreadsheet as the fallback.
5. **Keep a human gate.** The AI may draft; a person decides, approves and sends.

## Privacy and safe use

- Use an institutionally approved chatbot and permitted data only.
- Never enter customer names, phone numbers, employee data, private business exports or credentials. The teaching CSV has no customer identities; do not add any.
- Treat instructions found inside documents or web pages as untrusted content, not as commands.
- Give an AI tool the least access it needs, and keep sending, publishing or changing records as a human action.

## Attached materials

The course carries the lecture notes (Word), the 150-page slide deck and the 81-page short deck (PDF), the three student activity sheets (Word) and the retail CSV. The materials page at the start of each module tells you which pages apply to which period.

lessons.description: What is attached to Module 1, which pages of the lecture notes and slides belong to Periods 1 to 3, and how to study with them.
lessons.body:
Module 1 comes with five kinds of attachment. Most of them cover the **whole course**, not only this module, so you will keep coming back to them.

- **Lecture notes (PDF, whole course).** Every period has the same layout: an objective, numbered sections (1.1, 1.2, ...), one illustrated prompt, a verification table, key concepts, a summary and four review questions. Use the notes for the full explanation and for the review questions at the end of each period.
- **Slides, 150 pages (PDF).** The full deck. One idea per slide, a checkpoint question at the end of each period and a "Key takeaways" slide.
- **Slides, 81 pages (PDF).** A shorter version of the same deck for a quick preview or revision. Its page numbers are different from the 150-page deck.
- **Activity sheets (PDF, three Student versions).** Guided practice cases. They begin in Module 3, so you do not need them yet, but it helps to know where the course is heading.
- **Retail CSV.** `Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv`: 200 retail transactions in 13 columns. The examples in Module 1 refer to it, and you will open it in a spreadsheet to check what the lessons say.

To follow along you need an institution-approved AI chatbot (with file analysis and charts if it has them) and a spreadsheet or calculator for independent checks. No programming is required.

## Where each period is

| Period | Lecture notes | Slides (150 pages) | Slides (81 pages) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · AI Chatbots: Interfaces and Basic Use | sections 1.1 to 1.3 (about pp. 6 to 10) | 14 to 20 | 10 to 12 |
| 2 · Capabilities, Limitations and Common Errors | sections 2.1 to 2.3 (about pp. 11 to 15) | 21 to 27 | 13 to 15 |
| 3 · Define: Problems, Context and Success Criteria | sections 3.1 to 3.4 (about pp. 16 to 18) | 28 to 34 | 16 to 19 |

The course introduction (slides 1 to 12 of the long deck, and the first slides of the short deck) is also part of Period 1: it covers why a polished AI report can hide limited learning, who owns which responsibility, and the five-step cycle.

## How to use them

1. **Before a period:** skim its slides to see the shape of the lesson.
2. **In the lesson:** try every "Predict before you read" and "Find the error" box yourself before you open the answer, then take the quiz and rate your confidence for each question.
3. **After the quiz:** read the matching sections of the lecture notes and answer its four review questions in your own words.
4. **Check with the CSV:** every lesson ends with a "Check it yourself" task. Do it in a spreadsheet, not in a chatbot.
5. **For revision:** use the flashcards at the end of each lesson, then go back to the slides.

> [!meo] The prompts and AI answers in the notes and slides are **illustrative**: invented examples written to teach, not transcripts of a real AI session. Your chatbot will answer differently, which is exactly why you check what it gives you.

> [!ghi-nho] The course follows one cycle: **Define, Design, Execute, Evaluate, Refine**. Module 1 prepares the first two steps and the habit that runs through all of them: checking an AI result against evidence before you use it.

Choose an output format (text, table or chart) that fits a given question and reader

lessons.body:
A regional manager sends you a spreadsheet of 200 retail transactions and one line: *"Can you tell me how the regions are doing? Use the AI tool."* You open a chatbot. What do you type, what do you attach, what do you expect back, and what will you check before you pass anything on?

This period gives you the basic moves: choose an **input** the chatbot can really use, choose an **output** that suits the question, tell language help from data analysis, and keep your own responsibility for checking.

> [!ghi-nho] A chatbot works only with what it actually receives. Name the input, name the output, and keep the checking for yourself.

:::Predict before you read
A classmate types: *"Analyse Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv and tell me which region is best."* The chatbot answers at once with a confident table. Write down **two things that may be wrong** before you read on. You will come back to your list in the first worked example.
:::

sections.title: Choose the input
sections.intro: A chatbot can only work with what it actually receives. The input must contain the **evidence for the task**: the typed request, an attached document, an image, or a CSV where your product supports it. Availability depends on the chosen product, your account, your organisation and your permissions, so inspect what is enabled before you start.

parts.title: Text
parts.md: The task and its context, typed in your own words. Always needed, whatever else you attach.

parts.title: Documents
parts.md: A PDF or Word file, when the tool can open it. Right for "summarise this policy" or "check this report".

parts.title: Tables
parts.md: A CSV or Excel file, when file analysis is enabled. Right for questions about numbers such as regional totals.

parts.title: Images and voice
parts.md: A screenshot of a chart, or a spoken prompt, where the product accepts them. A screenshot shows a picture of numbers, not the data behind them.

sections.outro:
Some products also offer ways to reuse instructions (skills), find sources (research), group chats and files (projects) and create slides or PDFs. Treat these as optional extras that depend on your tool and account.

> [!canh-bao] A filename mentioned in chat is not the file. "Analyse Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv" gives the model a name, not 200 transactions.

sections.title: When the tool cannot open your file
sections.intro: Sometimes the chatbot you are allowed to use cannot read a CSV. This is normal, and it has a clean fallback.

parts.title: Do not
parts.md:
- Assume the file was uploaded because you mentioned it.
- Ask for a calculation on a file the tool has never seen.
- Accept a regional total that appeared from nowhere.

parts.title: Do
parts.md:
- Check for the attach control, or ask the tool what it can read.
- Calculate the numbers in a spreadsheet, then give the chatbot a small, verified extract or summary and say where it came from.
- Record the limitation, so that nobody thinks the chatbot analysed the file.

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] An imagined analysis can look exactly like a real one. If the tool cannot access the attachment, fix the access or supply a verified summary. Never accept an analysis of data it did not receive.

sections.title: Choose the output
sections.intro: Ask for a result the system can produce and your reader can use. Choose it by the question, not by what looks impressive.

parts.title: Text
parts.md: For definitions, explanations and short summaries. *Example: "Explain what each column of the dataset holds."*

parts.title: Table
parts.md: For exact values and rankings. *Example: a four-row table of regional net sales.*

parts.title: Chart
parts.md: For seeing a comparison across categories at a glance. *Example: a bar chart of regions.*

sections.outro: Charting depends on the tools enabled in your interface. If there is none, a clear **chart specification** (what goes on each axis, which labels, which values) is a valid fallback, and you can draw the chart in a spreadsheet.

parts.md:
One chat window supports very different jobs, and each job has its own evidence and its own quality check.

**Language and structure.** Explain, translate, summarise or organise information; draft and compare ideas; critique a response; extract named fields, classify descriptions or turn text into a table. You can read the answer and judge it against a source.

**Data work with enabled tools.** Inspect uploaded columns, summarise by category, draft a chart and follow-up questions. A claim about sales must be checked against the data that produced it, so you check file access, measure definitions and grouping, and reconcile the numbers to the source.

| Need | Suitable input | Useful output | Your check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Understand an unfamiliar idea | A question and a reliable excerpt | Plain-language explanation | Compare it with the excerpt |
| Summarise a document | The actual document or permitted text | Short summary with source pointers | Check key claims and omissions |
| Compare regional sales | The retail CSV or verified aggregated data | Four-row table, then a bar chart | Recalculate totals and labels |
| Prepare a management brief | Verified results and a defined decision | Findings, limitations and options | Review every claim and approval step |

> [!ghi-nho] The same chatbot can do all four jobs, but accuracy depends on the task, the context and the tools enabled. A common failure is to send a complex request before the input and the success criteria are clear. **Start small, so that you can check the result.**

sections.title: Worked example: a first conversation with the retail CSV
sections.intro: A manager wants a reliable overview of net sales by region. The input is the retail CSV. The first output should be a four-row table, **not** a business strategy. This is an illustrative exchange, not a transcript of a real session.

parts.title: Turn 1: inspect before you analyse
parts.md:
```html
Prompt (turn 1)
I have attached a retail transaction CSV. First list the column names and the number of records. Then explain which column represents net sales and which column identifies the region. Do not calculate profits or invent dates or currency. Ask me to confirm the task before making a chart.
``` **Why it works.** It names the input, asks for one small thing you can check, forbids the usual inventions (profit, dates, currency) and ends with a confirmation step so you stay in control.

parts.title: Read the reply against the file
parts.md:
A good reply identifies `Store_Region` and `Net_Sales_Amount`, confirms **200 records**, and names what is missing: no transaction date, currency, store identifier, cost or profit. It does not claim that the chain is profitable.

If the tool reports a different row count, find out why: was the header row counted, or were records filtered during import? If it cannot access the attachment, attach it again or supply a verified summary. Do not accept an imagined analysis.

parts.title: Turn 2: ask for the table
parts.md:
```html
Prompt (turn 2)
Now make a table with three columns: Store_Region, number of transactions and total Net_Sales_Amount. State the method you used. Then check that the four regional totals add up to the overall total of Net_Sales_Amount.
``` **Why it works.** Every step can be verified independently in a spreadsheet, and the last sentence builds in a reconciliation check.

parts.title: Compare with a weak request
parts.md:
```html
Prompt B (weak)
Analyse my sales file and tell me everything important.
``` **Why it is weak.** It does not say what the input is, which columns matter, what output you want or how you will judge the result. Whatever comes back, you would have no way to tell whether it is right.

sections.outro:
> [!vi-du] The conversation has two small turns instead of one big request. After turn 1 you know what the tool really sees. After turn 2 you have numbers you can recalculate.

**Back to your prediction.** The classmate's request had at least three weak points: the file may never have reached the chatbot (a name is not a file), the word "best" does not say which measure to use, and nothing in the request makes the answer checkable. You will fix the second one in Period 3.

sections.title: Who owns what
sections.intro: Imagine a student who asks AI to finish a whole data project. The model may return a polished document with headings and charts. Appearance cannot show whether the student understands the measures, whether the chart values are correct, or whether a recommendation follows from the numbers.

parts.title: AI can assist
parts.md:
- Suggest a plan
- Explain methods
- Draft tables and charts
- Challenge a claim

parts.title: You own
parts.md:
- Define the task and what success means
- Verify the numbers
- Interpret the limitations
- Approve the decision

sections.outro:
A better way to work is to ask for guidance in small steps, repeat one important calculation yourself, explain a chart in your own words and record how it was checked. ```html
Learn-with-AI prompt
Guide me through a regional sales analysis. First ask what I need to learn. Explain how to calculate one metric with the attached data. Ask me to check it before creating the chart. Explain each step so I can repeat it.
``` **Why it works.** It asks the AI to teach, not to hand over a finished report, and it puts a check by you between the AI's step and the next one. > [!canh-bao] A polished report is not evidence that you understand the work. The test is whether you can explain the method and repeat the calculation without the tool.

sections.title: The five-step cycle
sections.intro: The whole course uses one cycle. You may repeat it several times; a prompt is useful only when the result satisfies the real task. Here it is on one small task: *a manager can review one region this week.*

parts.title: Define
parts.md: Set the task and the success criteria. *Find the region with the lowest total net sales.*

parts.title: Design
parts.md: Write a clear request. *Ask for net sales totals and a ranking of all four regions.*

parts.title: Execute
parts.md: Run it in a suitable tool. *Run with the CSV; read the table and the method.*

parts.title: Evaluate
parts.md: Check the response against the task and the evidence. *Check the totals. Is it fewer purchases or lower sales per purchase?*

parts.title: Refine
parts.md: Change the request or workflow based on what failed or what you learned. *Ask for transaction counts and net sales per purchase, rerun and check again.*

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] Asking for counts **after** you have checked a ranking is Refine, not Execute: the request changes because of what the check showed.

parts.md:
Open the retail CSV in a spreadsheet and confirm what this lesson told you about it. Do not ask a chatbot to do these checks.

1. Count the rows of data (without the header) and the columns. Do you get **200** and **13**?
2. Is `Transaction_ID` different in every row?
3. Which columns could identify a region, a product category, a payment method and a customer type?
4. Look for a date, a currency, a store identifier, a cost and a profit column. Which of them exist?
5. Build a pivot table: `Store_Region` as rows, count of `Transaction_ID` and sum of `Net_Sales_Amount` as values. Do the four regional sums add up to the sum of the whole column?

:::Open after you have tried
The file has 200 transactions and 13 columns, and `Transaction_ID` is unique. The region column is `Store_Region` and the sales measure is `Net_Sales_Amount`. There is no date, currency, store, cost or profit column, so the year in the filename does not give any transaction a date. The four regional sums must add up to the grand total, since each transaction belongs to exactly one region.
:::

parts.title: My chatbot has no chart feature. Is the exercise ruined?
parts.md: No. Ask it for a chart specification, or build the chart in your spreadsheet from a table you have verified. Say clearly which tool did what.

parts.title: The chatbot explained its method clearly. Does that show it ran the calculation?
parts.md: No. Fluent text is not evidence that a calculation or a file check took place. Ask for the method, then reproduce one result yourself.

parts.title: If the AI got the numbers right, did I learn anything?
parts.md: Only if you can explain how the numbers were obtained and repeat the work with new inputs. Ask for steps you can follow, and try them.

parts.title: Who approves a recommendation that AI helped to draft?
parts.md: The responsible person: you or the manager. A chatbot, a template or a chart tool can produce the draft, but none of them is accountable for the decision.

items.meaning: A conversational system that responds to the inputs you supply.
items.example: You type a question and attach a CSV; it returns a table.

items.meaning: The instruction or material that directs the response.
items.example: "List the column names and the number of records."

items.meaning: The source information made available to the tool for the task. It must contain the evidence the task needs.
items.example: The attached CSV, or a verified four-row summary.

items.meaning: The text, table, chart or other result returned. Choose it by the question and the reader.
items.example: A four-row table to rank four regions.

items.meaning: An independent check against trusted evidence, not against the chatbot's own explanation.
items.example: Recalculating a regional total in a spreadsheet.

items.meaning: A name mentioned in chat is not the file. The tool needs the file or its contents.
items.example: Typing the CSV's name does not give the model any transactions.

items.meaning: What you do when the tool lacks a feature: supply a verified summary, or ask for a chart specification.
items.example: Pivot table in a spreadsheet, then paste the four rows.

items.meaning: The five-step cycle used throughout the course. Repeat it until the result satisfies the real task.
items.example: Asking for transaction counts after checking a ranking is Refine.

summary: Give the chatbot the actual evidence (file, extract or verified summary) and the output you want; a filename is not the file.
Choose text, table or chart by the question: tables for exact values, charts for comparisons, text for explanations.
Language help is judged against a source; a data claim is checked against the data that produced it.
The learner or manager owns the decision; a polished report does not show understanding, so explain and repeat the work.

questions.prompt: A student wants a chatbot to review a spreadsheet. Which input is most useful?
questions.explanation: The task depends on the values in the cells, so the chatbot needs the actual spreadsheet. A filename, a cover image or a timetable file does not contain those values. The filename is the tempting wrong answer: it identifies the file but is not the file.

questions.prompt: A manager needs a quick ranking of four regions. Which output suits the request?
questions.explanation: A ranking of four regions compares four values, so a four-row table shows it directly. An essay buries the ranking in prose, and spoken introductions or stock images contain no comparable values. A narrative suits an explanation; this request asks for a comparison.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant can read text but has no enabled file tool. What should the student do?
questions.explanation: Without a file tool the model cannot read your file, so the workable fallback is to paste a small, relevant extract (or a verified summary) and say that is what it is. Assuming an upload, asking for a calculation on an unseen file or accepting an invented total all depend on data the model never received.

options.label: Provide a small relevant data extract

questions.prompt: Who should approve a business recommendation drafted with AI?
questions.explanation: The responsible person stays accountable for decisions and evidence. The chatbot that wrote the draft is the tempting answer, but drafting, templating or rendering a recommendation does not give anyone or anything decision authority.

questions.prompt: Two students produce polished reports. What best tests their understanding?
questions.explanation: Reproducing a calculation tests whether the student knows the method. Cover design, paragraph counts and fluent headings measure presentation, which AI can make strong without any understanding behind it.

options.label: Ask them to reproduce a calculation
Count the paragraphs in each report
Rate the fluency of the headings

questions.prompt: After checking an AI-produced regional ranking, the manager asks for transaction counts. Which cycle stage is this?
questions.explanation: The ranking has already been run and checked, so the manager is changing the request because of what the check showed. That is Refine. Execute is tempting because a new request is run again, but the stage is decided by why you ask, not by the fact that you run it.

questions.prompt: Put the five stages of the course cycle in the correct order.
questions.explanation: You define the task and its success criteria first, then design the request, run it, evaluate the result against the task and the evidence, and refine what failed. The cycle can repeat several times.
sequence: Define: set the task and the success criteria
Design: write a clear request
Execute: run it in a suitable tool
Evaluate: check the response against the task and the evidence
Refine: change the request or workflow based on what failed

questions.prompt: If you mention the filename of a CSV in your message, the chatbot can analyse that file.
questions.explanation: False. A filename mentioned in chat is not the file. The file has to be attached (where your tool supports it) or its contents supplied, for example as a verified summary. Otherwise any numbers in the reply are invented.

questions.prompt: Which column of the retail CSV holds the net sales value of each transaction? Type the exact column name.
questions.explanation: The column is Net_Sales_Amount. Store_Region identifies the region of the sale; it does not hold an amount. Using exact field names in a prompt helps you check that the tool used the right column.

lessons.title: Period 2 · Capabilities, Limitations and Common Errors
lessons.description: Understand in simple terms how a language model builds an answer, decide what to delegate and what to keep, recognise unsupported or misleading output, and choose the right check or correction.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Explain in simple terms how a language model builds an answer from tokens, and why fluent text does not prove that an answer is true
Decide which parts of a task to delegate to AI and which to keep (source verification, reconciliation, decisions)
Recognise invented facts or citations, wrong quantities or labels, overinterpretation and task drift in a response
Test an AI statement against the retail CSV and decide whether to correct, qualify or remove each claim
Choose the check that suits each type of error
Rewrite a claim with the level of certainty that the evidence supports
lessons.body:
A colleague pastes this line from an AI tool into the team chat:

> *"East performed badly in October because demand fell. The region lost money and needs an immediate promotion."*

It reads like analysis: confident, specific and well put. This period teaches you to look at a sentence like that and ask a different question: **which parts of it can the data actually support?** You also learn, in simple terms, why an AI answer can be fluent and wrong at the same time.

> [!ghi-nho] An AI response can be useful without being fully reliable. Find the kind of error, run the check that fits it, and rewrite the claim with the level of certainty the evidence supports.

:::Predict before you read
Count the separate claims in the sentence above. For each claim, name the column you would need in the retail CSV to check it. Which claims have no matching column? Write your answer down, then compare it with the worked example below.
:::

sections.title: What to delegate and what to keep
sections.intro: Delegate the work where a draft is useful and a mistake is easy to spot. Keep the work where a mistake would go unnoticed and cost you.

parts.title: Useful to delegate
parts.md:
- Explaining a concept
- Drafting, outlining and rewriting
- Categorising and comparing alternatives
- Organising steps
- Exploratory suggestions

parts.title: Keep for yourself
parts.md:
- Verifying sources
- Reconciling numbers
- Accepting a claim
- Approving a policy or deciding an intervention

sections.outro: Some systems can also run calculations or inspect files when the right tools are enabled. A real data-analysis tool changes what the chatbot can calculate, but a text-only answer should **not** be presented as a computed result unless there is a recorded computation or a trusted source. Inspect your chosen interface instead of assuming that every chatbot behaves in the same way.

sections.title: How an AI answer is built

parts.md:
In simplified terms, a language model reads your prompt as **tokens**, which are pieces of text, and generates a response from patterns learned in training and from the information supplied in the conversation. Tokens are units of processed text. They are not facts, and they do not carry a guarantee of truth.

That is why natural, persuasive language does not prove anything. An answer can be consistent, convincing and wrong. It also explains two habits you will practise all course: **give the model the source information** it needs, and **check important results independently**.

> [!ghi-nho] Fluent text is not evidence that a calculation, a source check or an external action actually took place.

sections.title: Four common problems, four different checks
sections.intro: These are different problems and each calls for a different action. Poor formatting usually needs a targeted follow-up, not a redesign of the whole task.

parts.title: Invented facts or citations
parts.md:
A plausible reference, or a confident statement your source does not support.

**Check:** open the source, verify the title and the passage, and remove what you cannot verify.

parts.title: Wrong quantities or labels
parts.md:
A regional total is miscalculated, or a chart shows net sales but labels the axis "profit".

**Check:** recalculate with a formula and compare with the source column.

parts.title: Overinterpretation
parts.md:
A low recorded total is called "weak demand" although store coverage and time period are unknown.

**Check:** write it as a hypothesis and ask for the missing evidence.

parts.title: Task drift
parts.md:
The answer wanders from the requested four-row table into a long strategy discussion.

**Check:** compare the output with your success criteria and tighten the output instruction.

sections.outro: The slides add two more problems to keep in mind. **Bias:** the model may repeat stereotypes or judge a whole group unfairly. **Context limits:** it may miss relevant context, misread the request or rely on outdated information, for example an old policy applied to a current question.

sections.title: Worked example: check the East statement
sections.intro: The statement is an *illustrative faulty claim*, not an observed model response. The retail CSV records net sales by region and has no dates, no costs and no demand study.

parts.title: Split the sentence into claims
parts.md:
1. East performed badly.
2. ... in October.
3. ... because demand fell.
4. The region lost money.
5. It needs an immediate promotion.

parts.title: Test each claim against the file
parts.md:
| Claim | Supported by the CSV? | Reason and what is missing |
|---|---|---|
| East performed badly | Not as stated | The CSV gives recorded net sales per region. "Badly" needs a comparison standard such as a target or a past period, and the file has neither |
| In October | No | There are no transaction dates |
| Because demand fell | No | No demand measure and no time series; a comparison is not a cause |
| Lost money | No | There are no costs, so profit cannot be computed |
| Needs an immediate promotion | No | An action proposal without a trade-off analysis |

parts.title: Send a correction prompt
parts.md:
```html
Correction prompt
Review the statement using only the attached CSV. Make a table with four columns: claim, supported by the CSV (yes/no), reason, and information needed. Use the exact field names. Do not infer profit, dates, demand or causal effects. Rewrite the conclusion using verified observations only.
``` **Why it works.** It limits the evidence to the file, fixes the table layout, names the things the model must not infer, and asks for a rewrite, so you get a corrected sentence and not another lecture.

parts.title: Accept only what you can verify
parts.md: An acceptable rewrite: *"East has the lowest recorded regional net sales in this file."* Even that must be checked against the four totals, and it describes the data only. It says nothing about a time trend or the reason for the difference.

sections.outro:
> [!vi-du] The first response to a faulty claim is not to argue with the tool. It is to **separate the measurable observation from the rest of the sentence**.

> [!canh-bao] Words such as "profit", "declined", "caused" and "because" each ask for evidence. Check that the file has it before you let them stay.

sections.title: Find the error in this AI response

parts.md:
Here is another illustrative AI answer. Check it against the retail CSV and decide, claim by claim, whether to **correct**, **qualify** (state the limits) or **remove** it. Try before you open the answer.

> [!ghi-nho] *"West has net sales of 260,026.33, making it the most profitable region. Discounts caused its strong performance, as confirmed by a recent market report."*

Ask yourself: Does the figure belong to the stated region? Can net sales say which region earns the most profit? What evidence would support the story about discounts? Can you find and open the cited report?

:::Open after you have tried
**The figure.** 260,026.33 is the total for North, not West. Sum `Net_Sales_Amount` for each `Store_Region` and see for yourself. *Correct* the label.

**"Most profitable".** Net sales is not profit, and the file has no cost data. *Remove* the profit claim, or say that profit cannot be computed.

**"Discounts caused its strong performance".** The file has discount fields, but a comparison of totals does not show a cause. *Qualify* it as an untested hypothesis, and say what you would need to test it.

**"Confirmed by a recent market report".** No report is named, so nobody can open it. *Remove* it unless you can find the real source and check that it says this.
:::

sections.title: Match the problem to the response

parts.md:
| Output problem | Example | Appropriate response |
|---|---|---|
| Unsupported source | An article title is invented | Find an authentic source or remove the assertion |
| Arithmetic mismatch | Regional sums do not reconcile | Recalculate independently and correct the table |
| Ambiguous measure | "Best-performing region" | Define what "best" means: sales, profit, volume ... |
| Missing data | A profit figure with no cost data | State that profit cannot be computed |
| Excessive confidence | "The discount caused the decline" | Relabel it as an untested hypothesis |

**Check each corrected claim.** For every substantive answer ask:

- Did the tool actually receive the evidence?
- Are the units, the time period and the measure defined?
- Can a named source be opened and checked?
- Does the conclusion match the calculation?
- Does the wording imply a cause where the data shows only a comparison?
- Is the answer useful for the decision you need to make?

Record a correction as a new prompt. If the original question is impossible to answer with the data, revise the task brief instead (you do this in Period 3).

Use the retail CSV in a spreadsheet, not a chatbot.

1. Make a pivot table of the sum of `Net_Sales_Amount` by `Store_Region`. Which region is lowest? Is the figure 260,026.33 in the table, and for which region?
2. Look for a column that could confirm the word "October", the word "profit" or the word "demand". Which of them does the file have?
3. Write one question that the CSV **can** answer and one that it **cannot**, in your own words.

:::Open after you have tried
East should come out lowest, and 260,026.33 belongs to North. The file has no date, cost or demand column. A question it can answer: *Which region has the highest total net sales?* One it cannot: *Which region lost money in October?*
:::

parts.title: Does a citation make a claim trustworthy?
parts.md: No. A neat reference can be invented. Open the source and check that it exists and says what the answer claims.

parts.title: Should I stop using AI for anything with numbers?
parts.md: No. That would swap one mistake for another. Use a tool that really computes, keep a record of how, and recalculate the results that matter in a spreadsheet.

parts.title: When do I qualify a claim and when do I remove it?
parts.md: Qualify it when part of it is supported but the cause or the scope is not. Remove it when it is unsupported and you cannot verify it, such as a source nobody can open.

parts.title: Can I ask the AI whether its own answer is correct?
parts.md: You can ask it to list assumptions or to recheck a step, but its reassurance is not evidence. The check has to come from the source, a recalculation or a human review.

items.meaning: A model that generates language from patterns it learned and from the information supplied in the conversation.
items.example: It continues text in a plausible way; it is not a database of verified facts.

items.meaning: A unit of text that the model processes. A token is a piece of text, not a guaranteed fact.
items.example: A word, or part of a word.

items.meaning: Unsupported or fabricated content presented as if it were fact.
items.example: A citation to an article that does not exist.

items.meaning: A response that moves away from the agreed task.
items.example: A four-row table request that turns into a strategy essay.

items.meaning: A claim that one factor produced another. It needs suitable evidence, not just a comparison.
items.example: "The discount caused the decline."

items.meaning: Reading more into the data than it shows. Fix it by labelling a hypothesis and asking for the missing evidence.
items.example: Low recorded sales described as weak demand.

items.meaning: The three ways to handle a claim: fix a wrong fact, state the limits of a partly supported one, or delete an unsupported one.
items.example: Correct the region label; qualify the cause; remove the unnamed report.

items.meaning: A check that does not depend on the AI's own explanation: open the source, recalculate, or review as a human.
items.example: Summing Net_Sales_Amount per region in a spreadsheet.

summary: A language model builds an answer from tokens and learned patterns; fluent wording is not evidence that anything was verified or computed.
Delegate drafting, explaining and organising; keep source checking, reconciliation and decisions.
Name the problem first (invented source, wrong number, overinterpretation, task drift), then run the check that fits it.
Rewrite claims with the certainty the evidence supports: correct, qualify or remove.

questions.prompt: In the course explanation, what is a token?
questions.explanation: The model processes text in token units, which are pieces of text. A token is not a chart axis, an approval or a stored transaction record, even though all of these appear in analysis work.

questions.prompt: An AI answer invents a publication that cannot be found. What problem is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Inventing a source is a hallucination, a fabricated citation. The other options describe display or ordering problems, which are real but concern how correct information is shown, not whether the evidence exists.

questions.prompt: The chatbot asserts that East's low sales prove weak demand. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: The CSV cannot establish causes, store coverage or profit, so the cause must stay a hypothesis until more evidence supports it. Saying East had fewer stores or low profit just swaps one unsupported explanation for another, and reporting demand as fact is the original mistake.

options.label: State that East had fewer stores
Report demand as a measured fact

questions.prompt: A learner asks AI to provide a regional explanation. Which task should the learner retain?
questions.explanation: Human review is essential because a fluent explanation can go beyond the evidence. Asking the AI to certify itself or to approve the conclusion hands the check to the party being checked, and inventing missing dates adds new claims instead of testing the old ones.

options.label: Ask AI to certify its own accuracy
Judge whether the evidence supports it

questions.prompt: Why should a plausible AI-generated number be checked?
questions.explanation: Language quality and factual accuracy are separate. Any number, however plausible, needs a check. The other options invent blanket rules about length or format: long answers and tables can be accurate, and charts can represent data.

questions.prompt: A response contains a correct region total and an invented explanation for it. What is the best edit?
questions.explanation: The evidence supports the verified total but not the story about it, so keep the number and qualify the explanation. Replacing the story with a guess keeps the problem, keeping both treats speculation as a finding, and deleting both without checking throws away good evidence.

options.label: Replace the explanation with a guess
Keep the total; qualify the explanation

questions.prompt: AI provides three sources for a claim; one link does not exist. What should be done first?
questions.explanation: Sources need independent checking, so verify each one. A citation that looks tidy, a link that probably moved or a claim that the AI repeats does not make a missing source exist.

options.label: Count how often AI repeats it

questions.prompt: If an AI answer explains a calculation fluently and in detail, that proves the calculation was actually run.
questions.explanation: False. Fluent text is not evidence that a calculation, a source check or an external action took place. Ask for a recorded computation or a trusted source, and recalculate one result yourself.

questions.prompt: Match each output problem to the appropriate response.
questions.explanation: Each problem needs its own action. A source problem needs a source check, a sum needs arithmetic, an ambiguous word needs a definition, missing data needs an honest statement of the limit, and excessive confidence needs a relabelled hypothesis.

pairs.left: An article title that does not exist
pairs.right: Find an authentic source or remove the assertion

pairs.left: Regional sums that do not reconcile
pairs.right: Recalculate independently and correct the table
Define what "best" means: sales, profit, volume ...

pairs.left: A profit figure when the file has no costs
pairs.right: State that profit cannot be computed
Relabel it as an untested hypothesis

questions.prompt: A response moves away from the requested four-row table into a long strategy discussion. This problem is called task ______ (one word).
questions.explanation: Task drift: the answer leaves the agreed task. Compare the output with your success criteria and refine the output instruction, for example by repeating the required table layout and asking for nothing else.

lessons.title: Period 3 · Define: Problems, Context and Success Criteria
lessons.description: Turn a vague business concern into an answerable question, identify the audience and the evidence, describe the output and set testable success criteria before you write any prompt.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Turn a vague business concern into a narrow, answerable question
Name the audience, the decision and the available evidence, and say what is still missing
Tell whether a question can be answered with a given dataset
Write an expected output and success criteria that are observable and testable
Assemble a four-part task brief: question, context, expected result and success criteria
Decide what to do when a stakeholder asks for a measure the data does not contain
lessons.body:
The manager says: *"Our sales performance is disappointing."* A tempting reply is to type into a chatbot: *"Explain why my stores are doing badly and fix the problem."* It feels efficient. It is also a request that no data file can answer: it names no measure, it asks for a cause the data cannot show, and it demands an action nobody can justify yet.

This period is the first step of the cycle, **Define**. Before you write any prompt, you turn a vague concern into an answerable question, name the audience and the evidence, describe the output you want, and set success criteria you can test. The result is a four-part **task brief** that you carry into Period 4.

> [!ghi-nho] Define the decision and the available evidence first. A narrow, verifiable task is more useful than an instruction to "analyse everything".

:::Predict before you read
Imagine you may ask the manager three questions before you do any analysis. Which three would change your work the most? Write them down. Compare them with the three checks in the first section below.
:::

sections.title: From a vague concern to a first question
sections.intro: "Sales performance is disappointing" is a concern, not yet a task. Defining it stops the chatbot from filling the gaps with guesses. The brief should make sense to a fellow student who has not seen the conversation.

parts.title: Clarify the concern
parts.md: Compared with what: a target, a past period or another region? Does "sales" mean gross or net sales? What decision does the manager have to make?

parts.title: Check what the data can answer
parts.md: The CSV supports regional sales comparisons. It has no dates, targets or cost data, so it cannot establish a decline, a missed target or low profit.

parts.title: Agree on a first question
parts.md: *Which regions have the highest and the lowest total net sales?* Confirm with the manager that this comparison helps. Whether to change staffing or promotions is a **later** question that needs more evidence.

sections.title: Establish the context
sections.intro: Context is the audience, the decision and the evidence. For the regional task it comes out like this.

parts.title: Who needs the result?
parts.md: A retail manager preparing a short regional review.

parts.title: What decision needs support?
parts.md: Which regions deserve a closer look first.

parts.title: What data do we have?
parts.md: The retail transaction CSV, with `Store_Region` and `Net_Sales_Amount`: 200 transactions.

parts.title: What is still unknown?
parts.md: Targets, past sales trends, costs and the causes of any difference between regions. There are also no dates, store identifiers or currency.

sections.outro:
These four answers lead to one **answerable question**: *Which region has the highest and which the lowest sum of net sales?*

| Part of the brief | Question to ask | Retail example |
|---|---|---|
| Problem and question | What exactly are we answering? | Which region has the highest recorded total net sales? |
| Context and audience | Who needs this, and why? | A manager preparing a short regional review |
| Evidence and limits | What can we use and what is missing? | 200 transactions; no dates, costs, stores or currency |
| Output and success | What would a satisfactory answer contain? | A ranked four-row table with totals, a check and one caution |

sections.title: Define the output and the success criteria

parts.md:
**Expected result.** A table that ranks all four regions by total net sales, followed by two short observations.

| Rank | Region | Net sales |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Region A | ... |
| 2 | Region B | ... |
| 3 | Region C | ... |
| 4 | Region D | ... |

**Success criteria.**

- All four regions appear exactly once.
- The regional totals match the sums in the original CSV.
- The ranking and the labels are clear, and no currency is invented.
- Every observation is supported by the data.

> [!ghi-nho] An **output format** specifies the deliverable. **Success criteria** specify how to judge it. A useful criterion is observable, so you can see what to fix when it fails. Criteria can also cover readability and responsible claims.

> [!canh-bao] "Be useful", "sound confident" and "act as an expert" are not success criteria. You cannot check any of them against the file.

sections.title: Weak request or clarified brief?
sections.intro: The same manager, the same file, two very different starting points.

parts.title: Initial request
parts.md:
```html
Weak request
Explain why my stores are doing badly and fix the problem.
``` **Problems.** The measure is unspecified, the diagnosis ("badly") is unsupported and the action ("fix") cannot be justified from this CSV.

parts.title: Clarified brief
parts.md:
```html
Clarified brief
The manager needs to compare the four regions in the provided transaction file. Calculate total net sales and recorded transaction counts by region. Show a table sorted by net sales. Verify the totals against the file. Do not infer dates, profit or causes.
``` **Why it works.** It names the decision-maker, the measure, the grouping and the output, builds in a check, and keeps the result descriptive. Further diagnosis waits for more information.

sections.title: Assemble the four-part task brief
sections.intro: Write the brief once, in four parts, and keep it. In Period 4 you turn it into a prompt with the same question and the same expected result.

parts.title: 1. Problem and question
parts.md: Management needs a regional review. Which regions have the highest and the lowest total net sales?

parts.title: 2. Context
parts.md: A retail manager will use the result. Group by `Store_Region`; measure `Net_Sales_Amount`.

parts.title: 3. Expected result
parts.md: A ranked four-row table with two observations.

parts.title: 4. Success criteria
parts.md: Include every region; verify the sums; label clearly; avoid unsupported explanations.

sections.outro:
Read the brief like a contract:

- Can the task be answered with the specified source?
- Is the question precise?
- Are potentially misleading comparisons identified?
- Does a success test say how the check is done?

> [!canh-bao] If the manager later asks which region is most **profitable**, the scope has changed and the source is no longer adequate. Change the brief or obtain cost data. Do not ask the AI to estimate the missing measure.

sections.title: Let the chatbot help you define

parts.md:
You can complete the brief by hand before opening a chatbot, or you can ask the chatbot to question you first. ```html
Clarification prompt (illustrative)
Act as a task-planning assistant. Before analysing the retail CSV, ask up to four questions covering: the manager's decision, the target metric, the comparison groups, and the desired output. After I answer, produce a four-part task brief. Flag requirements that the file cannot support.
``` **Why it works.** It caps the number of questions, names what they must cover, asks for a defined result and tells the tool to point out what the file cannot support. **When to use it.** Use clarification when a missing detail would materially change the answer. If the task is already well defined, a long questionnaire only wastes time. The aim is to reduce uncertainty efficiently.

sections.title: Your turn: a brief for product categories

parts.md:
The manager now wants a one-page overview of retail net sales by **product category**. Write the four-part brief. Use the exact column names from the CSV.

:::Open the solution after you have tried
**1. Problem and question.** Which product category has the highest and which the lowest total net sales?

**2. Context.** A retail manager reviewing the product mix. Group by `Product_Category` (the file has four categories: Apparel, Electronics, Furniture, Grocery); measure `Net_Sales_Amount`. No dates, costs or currency are available.

**3. Expected result.** A ranked four-row table of total net sales by category, with two short observations.

**4. Success criteria.** Each category appears once; the four totals add up to the total of the whole file; the measure is named and no currency is invented; observations make no claim about profit, trend or cause.
:::

**Check it yourself.** In a spreadsheet, sum `Net_Sales_Amount` for the whole file, then by `Store_Region`. The regional sums must add up to the grand total, because every transaction has exactly one region.

:::Open after you have tried
The grand total of `Net_Sales_Amount` is **892,252.11**, with the currency unspecified. Use it only as your check. Do not paste it into a prompt that is meant to make the tool calculate it.
:::

parts.title: What if a stakeholder asks for profit and there is no cost data?
parts.md: Say that the file cannot support it. Change the question to one the data can answer, or obtain cost data. Never ask AI to estimate the missing measure.

parts.title: Two managers use the same dataset but need different decisions. Do they need different briefs?
parts.md: Yes. The data may be the same, but the success criteria must follow each decision.

parts.title: Should I always ask the chatbot to question me first?
parts.md: No, only when a missing detail would materially change the answer. A well-defined task does not need a questionnaire.

parts.title: Who is the brief written for?
parts.md: For anyone who has not seen your conversation, including you next week. If a classmate could not do the task from it, it is not finished.

items.meaning: A concise agreed description of the problem, audience, evidence and success, in four parts.
items.example: Question, context, expected result, success criteria.

items.meaning: A question the available data can actually answer.
items.example: Which region has the lowest total net sales?

items.meaning: A defined quantity used for comparison. "Best" is not a metric until you say which one.
items.example: Sum of Net_Sales_Amount per Store_Region.

items.meaning: A limit on scope or on what may be inferred.
items.example: Do not infer dates, profit or causes.

items.meaning: The shape of the deliverable.
items.example: A ranked four-row table with two observations.

items.meaning: An observable condition that shows whether the result meets the task. It tells you what to fix when it fails.
items.example: All four regions appear exactly once.

items.meaning: What the data contains and what it lacks. Naming the gaps stops the AI from filling them with guesses.
items.example: 200 transactions; no dates, costs, stores or currency.

items.meaning: A new question the original brief and data cannot support. Change the brief or get more data.
items.example: "Which region is most profitable?" when no costs exist.

summary: Define the decision first: ask what the manager must decide, which measure matters and which comparison is fair.
Context means the audience, the decision and the evidence, including what is missing from the data.
The output format names the deliverable; success criteria are observable checks that say how to judge it.
A four-part brief is a contract: if the stakeholder asks for something the data cannot support, change the brief or the data, not the facts.

questions.prompt: A retailer says, “Sales need attention.” What should be clarified first?
questions.explanation: A defined management decision tells you what to analyse. Chart colours, headings and the chatbot's persona are output choices that come after the problem is clear. The most tempting wrong answer is the chart colour because it feels concrete.

options.label: The color of the final chart

questions.prompt: The data include net sales by region but no sales targets. Which question is answerable?
questions.explanation: Regional net totals are in the file, so "which region has the lowest total" is answerable. Growth next month needs future data, a missed target needs targets, and the lowest profit needs costs. None of those is in the file.

options.label: Which region will grow next month?
Which region has the lowest profit?
Which region has the lowest total?

questions.prompt: Which criterion makes a task brief testable?
questions.explanation: A measurable output lets you check the result against the brief. Impressive personas, "be useful" and "sound confident" give you no pass or fail test.

options.label: A broad instruction to be useful

questions.prompt: A team drafts a retail brief without naming its audience. What revision helps most?
questions.explanation: The audience decides how much detail the result needs and what format suits it, so the missing audience is the requirement to add. A longer request, unrelated history or more synonyms add words but not the missing information.

options.label: State who will use the result

questions.prompt: A prompt asks for “the best region” from net sales alone. What is the central flaw?
questions.explanation: "Best" might mean the highest sales, the highest margin or the fastest growth, and each needs different evidence. The use of a comparison, the number of regions and the length of column names are not the source of the ambiguity.

options.label: The column names are too long

questions.prompt: Two managers share the same dataset but need different decisions. How should the prompts differ?
questions.explanation: Success criteria must follow the decision each manager faces. A shared dataset does not mean shared information needs. Removing context, letting the tool choose the objective or reusing one criterion all lose the link between the decision and the check.

options.label: Let the tool choose each objective
Match success criteria to each decision
Reuse the identical criterion for both

questions.prompt: A request for monthly sales trends uses the provided retail CSV. What missing input matters most?
questions.explanation: Monthly trends need a date on every record, and this file has none. A more detailed role, a shorter title or an example chart improve presentation but cannot supply missing data.

options.label: An example of a bar chart

questions.prompt: Match each part of the four-part task brief to its content in the regional example.
questions.explanation: The brief has four parts: the question, the context, the expected result and the success criteria. The question says what is being asked, the context says who and which data, the result is the deliverable, and the criteria are the checks.

pairs.right: Which regions have the highest and the lowest total net sales?
A retail manager will use it; group by Store_Region, measure Net_Sales_Amount
A ranked four-row table with two observations
Include every region, verify the sums, label clearly, avoid unsupported explanations

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks which region is the most profitable. The file has no cost data. The best next step is to ask the chatbot to estimate costs so the brief can stay the same.
questions.explanation: False. The scope has changed and the source cannot support it. Change the brief to a question the data can answer, or obtain cost data. Asking AI to estimate a missing measure invents evidence.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of defining a task in a sensible order.
questions.explanation: You start from the concern, clarify what it means, check what the data can answer, agree on a first answerable question, and only then write the expected result and the success criteria that make up the brief.
sequence: Hear the manager's concern
Clarify the decision, the measure and the comparison
Check what the available data can and cannot answer
Agree on a first answerable question
Write the expected result and the success criteria in a four-part brief

modules.title: Module 2 — Design: Prompts and Prompting Strategies
modules.description: Three periods on the Design step of the cycle: build a complete prompt from five functions, improve an answer with targeted follow-ups, and choose a prompting strategy (examples, clarification, explanation or chaining). Practised on the regional net-sales task, with every figure checked against the CSV.

lessons.title: Module 2 materials: lecture notes, slides and the retail CSV
lessons.description: Which attached files support Module 2, where Periods 4, 5 and 6 sit in each of them, and how to use them next to the three lessons.
lessons.body:
Module 2 comes with attached files written by the course team. They are a reference, not a prerequisite: each lesson stands on its own, and you open the files when you want the original wording, the full slide or the data.

## What is attached

| File | What it is | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Lecture notes (PDF, whole course) | The written text of all 14 periods. Each period has numbered sections (4.1, 4.2 ...), key concepts, a summary and four review questions | Reading the full explanation and trying the review questions |
| Slides, 150 pages (PDF) | The complete deck: one slide per idea, plus activity, "Review the prompts" and checkpoint slides | Seeing each prompt exactly as shown in class; the checkpoint questions |
| Slides, 81 pages (PDF) | A shorter deck with the core slides of the long one | A quick preview or revision |
| Activity sheets 1-3, Student versions (PDF) | The three guided activities of the course | Looking ahead only: Activity 1 starts at Period 7 (Module 3) |
| Retail sales CSV | 200 transactions with 13 columns, among them `Transaction_ID`, `Store_Region`, `Product_Category`, `Gross_Amount`, `Discount_Amount` and `Net_Sales_Amount` | Every "Check it yourself" box in this module |

> [!ghi-nho] The CSV has **no dates, no currency, no costs, no store coverage and no profit data**. That is deliberate: it is why you will keep seeing prompts that say "leave the currency unspecified" and "do not infer profit".

## Where each period is

| Period | Lecture notes | Slides (150 pages) | Slides (81 pages) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 Prompt Anatomy | Period 4, sections 4.1-4.5 | 37-45 | 20-24 |
| 5 Follow-up Prompts | Period 5, sections 5.1-5.5 | 46-55 | 25-31 |
| 6 Prompting Strategies | Period 6, sections 6.1-6.5 | 56-65 (references on slide 66) | 32-38 |

The longer deck also has the activity slides of this module ("Write a Category Prompt", "Refine the Answer", "Choose a Prompting Strategy"), the "Review the prompts" slide and the key takeaways for each period. The lessons contain the same activities.

## How to use them

1. **Before a period:** skim the matching slides to see the shape of the topic.
2. **In the lesson:** try each "Predict before you read" and "Find the error" box yourself before you open the answer, then take the quiz and rate your confidence for each question.
3. **Check it yourself:** open the CSV in a spreadsheet and recompute the figures named in the box. A pivot table or `SUMIF` is enough; no programming is needed.
4. **After the quiz:** read the matching section of the lecture notes and try its review questions.
5. **For revision:** use the flashcards at the end of each lesson, then return to the slides.

> [!meo] Where a chatbot cannot read files or draw charts, paste a verified table from your spreadsheet instead and write down that limitation. The module asks you to do this in several places.
summary: Module 2 is supported by the lecture notes, a 150-page deck, an 81-page deck and the retail CSV; the activity sheets start at Period 7.
The table shows where Periods 4, 5 and 6 sit in each file, and the CSV (no dates, currency, costs or profit) backs every check-it-yourself box.

lessons.title: Period 4 · Prompt Anatomy
lessons.description: Five functions of a prompt (instruction, context, input, output, constraints), how OpenAI, Google and Anthropic group them, and how to cut every sentence that does not earn its place.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Identify the instruction, context, input, output and constraints in a prompt
Build a complete task-specific prompt for a net-sales question using exact column names
Compare how OpenAI-, Google- and Anthropic-style layouts group the same requirements
Decide whether each sentence of a prompt changes an observable property of the answer, and cut it if not
Adapt a finished prompt to a new grouping and name one independent check
lessons.body:
Your Period 3 task brief is finished: a question (which regions have the highest and lowest total net sales?), a reader (a retail manager), an expected result (a ranked four-row table) and success criteria. Now you have to turn it into the message the chatbot actually receives. A brief is not yet a prompt: until the question, the evidence, the output and the limits are written into the message, the chatbot has to guess them.

> [!ghi-nho] A prompt is complete when it holds enough information to guide the task **and** to judge the answer. Nothing in a prompt, however well written, replaces checking the result.

:::Predict before you read
A colleague sends a chatbot only this: "Study this file." You may add one sentence. Which would help most: "You are a world-class analyst", "Sum net sales by region", or "Be thorough and professional"? Decide, then say what you could check in the answer for each choice. Compare with the table of optional elements below.
:::

sections.title: Five functions of a prompt
sections.intro: A useful prompt does five jobs. Their order can vary, and one sentence may do two jobs at once.

parts.title: Instruction
parts.md:
The action you request.

*Sum `Net_Sales_Amount` for each `Store_Region`.*

parts.title: Context
parts.md:
Who will use the answer and for what decision.

*A retail manager reviewing regional activity.*

parts.title: Input
parts.md:
The source material or data the answer must rest on.

*The attached retail CSV and its real column names.*

parts.title: Output
parts.md:
The format and content of the result.

*A four-row table, ranked highest to lowest, with two observations.*

parts.title: Constraints
parts.md:
Boundaries and quality rules.

*Include all regions; do not invent currency; do not infer profit or causes.*

sections.outro:
A **role** (who the assistant should act as) and **examples** are optional extras that help with some tasks. None of the five functions, and neither extra, replaces verifying the result.

> [!canh-bao] If the chatbot cannot open the CSV, the input is missing, however elegant the rest of the prompt sounds. Attach the file, paste a verified table, or say plainly that the data is not available.

sections.title: From a vague prompt to a complete one

parts.md:
Compare two prompts for the same job. ```html
Prompt A (weak)
Study this file.
``` **Why it is weak:** it names no metric, no grouping, no output and no limits. The chatbot must guess all four, and you cannot judge the answer because you never said what a right answer looks like. ```html
Prompt B (complete)
A retail manager needs to review sales performance across regions.
Using the attached retail CSV, sum Net_Sales_Amount for each Store_Region.
Return a four-row table with region, transaction count and total net sales, ranked from highest to lowest, then two short observations, one of which states a limitation of the data.
Check that the four regional totals add up to the total for the whole file.
The currency is not given in the file: leave it unspecified.
Include all regions. Do not infer profit, dates or the causes of regional differences.
``` **Why it works:** read it line by line and label each one. | Line of Prompt B | Function | |---|---| | A retail manager needs to review sales performance across regions. | Context | | Using the attached retail CSV, sum Net_Sales_Amount for each Store_Region. | Instruction and input | | Return a four-row table ... then two short observations ... | Output | | Check that the four regional totals add up to the whole-file total. | Constraint (a quality rule you can test) | | The currency is not given ... Do not infer profit, dates or causes. | Constraints (limits on claims) | The prompt makes the task checkable because it names the exact fields and asks for a reconciliation. A good answer has four regions, a correct total and restrained interpretation. **Two ways it can still fail.** The table might use `Gross_Amount` instead of `Net_Sales_Amount`, or the answer might say that North achieved the highest *profit*. Check the metric label and the figures, then revise the one instruction that failed instead of simply adding more words. > [!vi-du] The same prompt works for categories. Replace `Store_Region` with `Product_Category`, keep the calculation and the check, and you still get four groups. You will try this in "Your turn" below.

sections.title: Three providers, one set of ideas
sections.intro: The course adapts published prompting guidance from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic. Each groups the same needs under its own labels.

parts.title: OpenAI-inspired
parts.md:
**Identity**, **instructions**, optional **examples** and **context**.

Output and constraints sit inside the instructions; the data sits in the context. Identity sets the role.

parts.title: Google-inspired
parts.md:
**Input**, **instructions**, **context**, **constraints**, **response format**, and examples where useful.

The response format is what this course calls the output.

parts.title: Anthropic-inspired
parts.md:
An optional **role**, **clear instructions**, **context**, **source material**, and short examples only when needed.

The instructions include the output and the limits.

sections.outro:
For a beginner the three questions that matter stay the same under every layout: **Is the task clear? Is the needed evidence present? Is the output testable?**

> [!canh-bao] Do not memorise one template as if it were a rule. If two prompts hold the same task, data and restrictions but arrange them differently, you cannot tell which is better by looking at them. Run both, score the outputs against one rubric and keep what works.

sections.title: Optional elements: when they help, how they backfire

parts.md:
Role, examples, exact column names, an output schema and boundaries are all choices, not obligations.

| Element | Often useful when | Risk if misused |
|---|---|---|
| Role or audience | Tone or professional framing matters | Invents authority or competence |
| Examples | The output pattern is hard to describe | The model copies a misleading example |
| Exact column names | You are working with a file | You ask for fields that do not exist |
| Output schema | Reports must be comparable | A rigid but unhelpful structure |
| Boundaries | Sources are incomplete or sensitive | Over-broad bans block the task |

A role alone does not name the measure or stop invented explanations: the instruction must still say `Net_Sales_Amount` and the limits.

> [!ghi-nho] A longer prompt can be better, equal or worse than a short one. It may add conflicting instructions or accidental assumptions. For each sentence ask: *if I deleted this, what would change in the answer I can observe?* If nothing, delete it.

> [!meo] When two versions of a prompt look equally good, do not argue about wording. Give both the same data, score both answers on the same short rubric (right measure, four regions, totals reconcile, caveat visible) and keep the winner.

sections.title: Find the problems in this prompt

parts.md:
This prompt looks thorough. It is not. ```html
Prompt C (looks thorough)
You are the world's best retail data scientist with 30 years of experience. Please study the attached sales file very carefully and give me revenue in dollars for each region, plus how profit changed month by month. Be extremely detailed and professional. Do a great job.
``` Find at least five problems before you open the answer. :::Open the answer after you have tried 1. **The role claim** ("world's best ... 30 years") changes nothing you can check; it invents authority. 2. **"Revenue"** names no column. The file has `Gross_Amount` and `Net_Sales_Amount`, and they give different totals. 3. **"In dollars":** the CSV has no currency. The prompt invites a guessed unit. 4. **"Profit":** the file has no costs, so profit cannot be calculated or its change described. 5. **"Month by month":** the file has no dates, so no monthly view is possible. 6. **"Extremely detailed"** conflicts with a manager who needs a short answer, and no output format is given. 7. There is **no check** asked for, for example reconciling the regional totals with the file total. A fix is Prompt B: the same job with exact fields, the output shape, an unspecified currency and explicit limits. :::

sections.title: Your turn: write the category prompt

parts.md:
A new business question: **which product categories have the highest and lowest total net sales?** Using the regional prompt as a pattern, not as text to copy: 1. Write a short prompt that uses `Product_Category` and `Net_Sales_Amount`. 2. State who will use the answer and choose a suitable output format. 3. Include relevant limits and say how you would check the result. 4. Label the instruction, context, input, output and constraints in your own prompt. A role or an example is optional: add one only if it adds useful guidance. :::Open the model answer after you have tried ```html
Model category prompt
A retail manager wants to know which product categories to review first.
Using the attached retail CSV, sum Net_Sales_Amount for each Product_Category.
Return a four-row table with category, transaction count and total net sales, ranked from highest to lowest, then two short observations, one of which states a limitation of the data.
Check that the four category totals add up to the total for the whole file.
The currency is not given in the file: leave it unspecified.
Do not infer profit, dates or the reasons for differences between categories.
``` Only the grouping field changed. For your own check, the CSV gives: | Product_Category | Transactions | Net sales | |---|---|---| | Apparel | 54 | 259,252.42 | | Furniture | 51 | 231,255.44 | | Grocery | 49 | 201,931.10 | | Electronics | 46 | 199,813.15 | | **All** | **200** | **892,252.11** | :::

parts.title: Does every prompt need a role?
parts.md: No. A role is optional. It can help set tone or audience, but it cannot make an answer accurate. Include it only if it changes something you can observe.

parts.title: What is the difference between the instruction and the output?
