questions.explanation: 4,666.78 is an average of net sales over East's 39 records. It describes value per record, not margin, and the file has no costs, so it cannot show profitability. The other three statements correctly describe what the measure is.

options.label: The calculation uses East transactions only
The measure differs from total net sales
High transaction value proves high profitability
The amount is an average over records

questions.prompt: A table compares East product categories. Which accompanying statement best protects interpretation?
questions.explanation: East's categories have different counts (from 4 to 13) and each total mixes count and value, so a table should say that counts may affect total comparisons. Identical prices, seasonal shifts and equal market coverage are not established by the CSV.

options.label: The data establish seasonal category shifts
Each category has equal market coverage
Category counts may affect total comparisons

questions.prompt: Two sources agree on East's total but differ on why it is low. How should findings be reported?
questions.explanation: The total is a checked fact and the explanations are hypotheses. Report the total, label both explanations as competing hypotheses and say what data would separate them. Blending them, picking the more persuasive one, or calling them tested adds certainty the evidence lacks.

options.label: Present the total; flag competing hypotheses
Average the explanations into a single cause
State both causes were experimentally verified

questions.prompt: A manager asks for a root-cause report immediately. Which output is supportable now?
questions.explanation: With transaction-level fields you can give a descriptive diagnosis and list the data gaps. A proven causal model, a profit forecast or a store productivity ranking would need store, date, cost or experiment data that the file does not hold.

options.label: A preliminary diagnosis with data gaps
A proven causal model of demand

questions.prompt: Match each statement from the East claim register to its label.
questions.explanation: Counts and totals checked in the CSV are verified findings. A plausible explanation the file cannot test is a working hypothesis. The fields you would need to test it are missing inputs. A choice you postpone until evidence exists is a decision to defer.

pairs.left: East has 39 records and 182,004.38 net sales.
pairs.right: Verified finding

pairs.left: East may have fewer active stores or a shorter reporting window.
pairs.right: Working hypothesis

pairs.left: Store identifiers, extraction dates and opening days.
pairs.right: Missing input

pairs.left: Do not choose a promotion solely from regional totals.
pairs.right: Decision to defer

questions.prompt: All four regions together have 892,252.11 in net sales from 200 transactions. What is the overall net sales per transaction, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Divide the total by the total count: 892,252.11 / 200 = 4,461.26. The plain average of the four regional averages is 4,470.29, a different number, because it ignores that the regions have different record counts.

questions.prompt: East's Electronics subgroup has only 4 recorded transactions, so this proves that East's Electronics business is failing.
questions.explanation: False. Four records is a small subgroup and a candidate investigation point. It is a fact about what was recorded; it does not show a failure or a cause, and it can depend on which stores or periods the extract includes.

lessons.title: Period 11 · Develop Evidence-Based Options
lessons.description: Turn the East diagnosis into three investigative options, compare them on evidence and assumptions, challenge an attractive promotion idea and record a human choice.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Ask AI for three next-step options that each state the evidence they respond to, an unconfirmed assumption and the new information required
Compare options in a four-column table and judge which new data would most change the decision
Challenge an unsupported promotion proposal by naming two alternative explanations and a check for each
Explain why historical discount values in the CSV do not establish the effect of a future promotion
Record a human-approved direction with a justification and the findings that would change it
Check an AI option table against five questions before using it
lessons.body:
On Monday the manager reads your East diagnosis and says: "Good. Let's run a discount promotion in East next week." It sounds decisive, and an AI assistant will happily write the campaign.

Stop and list what you actually know. East has 39 recorded transactions, the fewest, and the highest net sales per transaction. The file has no store list, no dates, no costs and no campaign history. Nothing in it says *why* East has fewer records, or that a discount would change that.

> [!ghi-nho] At this stage ask AI for **next steps for investigation**, not for actions that spend money. A good option list shows what you would need to know in order to choose safely.

:::Predict before you read
The manager proposes a discount promotion for East. List two things, other than weak customer demand, that could explain East's low record count. Then write one check that could tell each of them apart from weak demand. You will compare your list with the challenge section.
:::

parts.md:
Ask for investigative options and make the AI expose what each one rests on. ```html
Prompt A — weak
What should we do to boost East sales?
``` **Why it is weak:** it assumes East needs a boost, asks for actions instead of investigations, and does not ask the AI to show evidence, assumptions or data needs. The answer will sound actionable and be impossible to check. ```html
Prompt B — option generation
Using the verified East diagnosis, suggest three useful next steps. For each, state the observed evidence it responds to, an unconfirmed assumption, and new information required. Include at least one data-coverage check. Keep sales interventions conditional on additional evidence.
``` **Why it is better:** the three fields it demands (evidence, assumption, new information) turn each option into something you can test, and the coverage check keeps the most basic question on the list. A suitable answer would suggest checking reporting coverage, comparing store-level activity and investigating customer acquisition **only if** a meaningful activity shortfall remains after that. These are proposed approaches, not results of any business experiment.

Put the options side by side so their evidence and assumptions are visible before you choose. ```html
Follow-up — comparison table
Put these options in a comparison table: option, current evidence, assumption to test, and information needed. Keep each entry brief; treat assumptions as unconfirmed.
``` | Option | Current evidence | Assumption to test | Information needed | |---|---|---|---| | Check source coverage | East has 39 records, the fewest | Source includes unequal periods or stores | Store list, dates, extraction rules | | Compare activity on a common basis | East's net sales per record is comparatively high | Stores may differ in activity | Store IDs, opening days, customer visits | | Investigate acquisition | East has fewer recorded transactions | Customer demand may be weaker | Traffic or visits, conversion, campaign costs | Every option has different prerequisites: - **Source-coverage check.** Conceptually simple, and it protects every later analysis. - **Common-basis comparison.** Needs a fair denominator, such as transactions per active store per operating day, *if* the organisation can supply and validate those fields. - **Acquisition analysis.** Needs evidence of demand, the costs, and a proper evaluation design before any claim about performance. Two test questions help you choose when only one check can be funded this week. Would the extra data **materially change the decision**? And what is the **information value relative to the effort**? An option that sounds impressive but cannot change what you do is a poor first choice. > [!canh-bao] The table must label assumptions as assumptions. If the "Assumption" column reads like a finding ("East demand is weaker"), the AI has smuggled a hypothesis in as evidence.

sections.title: Challenge an option
sections.intro: An AI may suggest: *"Run a discount promotion in East to increase purchases."* It is attractive because it sounds like action. A good reviewer asks what else could explain the problem and what is missing.

parts.title: Why the idea is attractive
parts.md:
- It is concrete and quick to explain
- East has the fewest records, so "more purchases" seems the obvious goal
- The CSV even contains discount columns, so it feels data-backed

parts.title: What the file does not contain
parts.md:
- Store identifiers and reporting dates, so coverage is unknown
- Costs, gross margin or profit
- Any experiment or campaign result
- Customer visits or traffic

Discounts are recorded only as past values on each transaction. They cannot show what a future promotion would do.

sections.outro:
```html
Challenge prompt
Challenge the proposal to run a promotion in East. Identify two alternative reasons for its smaller recorded transaction count. For each, state a check that could distinguish it from lower customer demand. Explain which facts must be established before we spend on a promotion.
``` **Why it works:** it asks for alternatives *and* a way to tell them apart, so the answer is a to-do list rather than an opinion. Two basic alternatives are **fewer stores represented in the extract** and **a shorter reporting period**. Checking store and time coverage is a prerequisite for any comparison. Even if East's count stays low after adjusting for coverage, customer traffic, pricing, product availability and competing conditions may matter. Do not say any of them is responsible until it has been measured. If you listed fewer stores, a shorter window or a different traffic level in the "Predict" box, you were on the right lines. Each of those has a check: the store list, the extraction dates, the visit counts. > [!vi-du] The CSV does show that East's overall discount rate (total `Discount_Amount` divided by total `Gross_Amount`) is 12.45%, the lowest of the four regions (North 13.32%, South 14.28%, West 15.97%). Someone could tell a story from that: "East discounts least, so fewer people buy." It is only a story. The file has no experiment, so it fits equally well with discounts being irrelevant to the count.

sections.title: Select a direction: the human decision gate
sections.intro: The AI may recommend, but a person chooses. The teaching example chooses **verify coverage first**. This is a human decision based on missing source information and the risk of misreading transaction counts. It is not proof that East has a coverage error.

parts.title: State the choice
parts.md: Name one direction in plain words: *check regional store and reporting coverage before any campaign.*

parts.title: Justify it with verified evidence
parts.md:
```html
Human-approved choice prompt
We choose to check regional store and reporting coverage before any campaign. Write a two-sentence justification using the verified East evidence. Then identify what outcome from the coverage check would justify a deeper sales investigation. Do not claim that the coverage problem has already been found.
``` A useful justification: *East has fewer recorded transactions while having the highest recorded net sales per transaction. Without comparable store and reporting-period coverage, these counts do not establish a demand problem.*

parts.title: Say what would change the choice
parts.md: For example: if the coverage check shows the same stores and the same period in every region, the low count is more likely to be real activity, and a deeper look at demand becomes justified.

parts.title: Record the decision
parts.md:
| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Direction chosen | Check coverage first |
| Chosen by | The manager or named decision owner |
| Evidence used | East: 39 records, 4,666.78 per transaction |
| Assumptions | Coverage may differ between regions |
| Deferred options | Promotion; acquisition analysis |
| What would change it | Matching coverage with the count still low |

sections.outro: > [!ghi-nho] The value of this choice is that the next analysis will be better specified. Save the options and challenge record, so a later reviewer can see why the promotion was deferred.

sections.title: Check the recommendation before use
sections.intro: Before you accept an AI option table, ask these five questions.

parts.title: 1. Traceable?
parts.md: Is every stated number or observation traceable to the CSV and a calculation you have seen?

parts.title: 2. Assumptions labelled?
parts.md: Does the table mark assumptions as assumptions, not as findings?

parts.title: 3. Requests necessary?
parts.md: Is each new data request needed to choose between the options?

parts.title: 4. Feasible follow-up?
parts.md: Does the proposal give a follow-up you can actually do, rather than an unsupported causal conclusion?

parts.title: 5. A person chose?
parts.md: Has a named person, not the chatbot, picked the next step?

parts.title: Is a coverage check just a way of delaying?
parts.md: No. It is cheap, it protects every later analysis, and it can change the decision. If East's low count turns out to be a coverage artefact, a promotion would have treated a data problem as a business problem.

parts.title: Can the AI choose between the options?
parts.md: It can rank and justify them, which is useful input. The choice, and the accountability for it, stays with the manager or designated decision owner.

parts.title: Two options cite the same East total but recommend opposite actions. How do I decide?
parts.md: Compare their assumptions and the evidence for each. Shared descriptive data can support different hypotheses, so the assumptions decide whether an action is justified. Do not average the two actions or pick the one that sounds more confident.

parts.title: What if an option needs data we do not have, such as customer visits?
parts.md: Keep it on the list as **contingent on new evidence**. You cannot estimate visits from transaction IDs, and you should not report the effect as proven.

1. In the spreadsheet, compute each region's discount rate as the sum of `Discount_Amount` divided by the sum of `Gross_Amount`. You should get East 12.45%, North 13.32%, South 14.28% and West 15.97%. Then write one sentence about what this does **not** show.
2. Take an AI-written option table and, for every number in it, find the cell or pivot that supports it. Any number you cannot trace is unverified.
3. Write two questions that would test whether East's 39 transactions are comparable to another region's count.

:::Find the error
An AI option list says: "Option 1: run a 15% discount in East. East customers respond poorly to current pricing, and this will raise transactions by about 12% within a month. Information needed: none, the CSV is sufficient."

Find at least three problems before you open this box.
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
1. "East customers respond poorly to current pricing" is an unlabelled assumption. Nothing in the CSV measures how customers respond to price.
2. "Raise transactions by about 12% within a month" is an invented forecast. There is no experiment, baseline or timing in the file.
3. "Information needed: none" is false. A promotion needs coverage, cost and demand evidence, and an evaluation design, none of which the CSV holds.
:::

items.meaning: A candidate course of action or investigation. At this stage, prefer investigations that expose what you would need to know.
A statement used for planning that has not been established. An option table must label assumptions as assumptions.
items.example: Customer demand may be weaker in East.

items.meaning: Another plausible account of the same observation.
items.example: East's smaller count could reflect fewer stores or a shorter reporting period.

items.meaning: Missing information that limits a conclusion, such as store IDs, dates or customer visits.
Option, current evidence, assumption to test and information needed, kept brief so differences are visible.
The best criterion when only one check can be funded: how much the answer would change the decision, against how hard it is to get.
A prompt that asks for alternative explanations and a check to tell them apart, to expose assumptions rather than to add certainty.
An explicit human approval before moving from options to action.
An option that depends on evidence you do not yet hold, so it stays a hypothesis to investigate.

summary: Produce options only after the evidence is understood, and ask for next investigative steps with their evidence, assumptions and information needed.
Compare options in a table where assumptions are labelled, then challenge the most attractive one: historical discount values cannot show what a future promotion would do.
A person chooses the direction and records why. In the East example, verifying store and reporting coverage comes first.
Check every AI option table for traceable numbers, labelled assumptions, necessary data requests, a feasible follow-up and a human choice.

questions.prompt: After diagnosing East's recorded sales, what should AI help generate?
questions.explanation: After a diagnosis, AI's job is to propose next investigation steps and what each would need. It cannot supply past dates the file lacks, guarantee a campaign result or approve spending; spending needs a person's approval.

questions.prompt: East appears to have low recorded activity. Which next step addresses comparability?
questions.explanation: Store counts and reporting coverage test directly whether East's recorded count is comparable with the other regions. Assuming equal stores, concluding that East has fewer customers, or raising prices all act on an explanation that has not been checked.

options.label: Check store counts and reporting coverage
Assume the sample contains equal stores
Conclude the region has fewer customers

questions.prompt: What should an options comparison make explicit?
questions.explanation: A comparison is useful when it shows what evidence each option needs, so you can see which ones can be tested now. Prompt length, colour preferences and the chatbot's writing style say nothing about the quality of an option.

options.label: The length of the generated prompt

questions.prompt: A manager can fund only one diagnostic check this week. Which criterion best guides selection?
questions.explanation: With one check to fund, choose the one whose answer would change the decision most for the effort it takes. Enthusiasm, length and the number of tool names are presentation, not value.

options.label: Which option has the longest description
Which option uses the most tool names

questions.prompt: AI suggests a discount campaign because East has low total sales. What challenge is most pertinent?
questions.explanation: The suggestion assumes discounts are linked to East's low total, and the CSV has no experiment or cost data to show that, so ask what evidence links them. Stronger wording or another chart colour changes presentation only, and a made-up baseline would be invented.

options.label: Can the recommendation use stronger adjectives?
Can the manager add a fictional baseline?
What evidence links discounts to the problem?
Would another chart color improve the claim?

questions.prompt: Three options each require different new inputs. What should the comparison table include?
questions.explanation: A comparison table should show the data each option needs, what it is likely to be worth and the effort it takes. Guaranteed financial effects cannot be known from this file, and headlines or popularity do not support a reasoned choice.

options.label: Only a persuasive headline per option
Required data, likely value and effort
Only estimated popularity and font style

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of challenging an AI-proposed option?
questions.explanation: Challenge makes hidden assumptions visible and shows what evidence is missing. It does not make a recommendation more certain, change the business question or throw away totals you have already verified.

questions.prompt: One option seems attractive but needs customer visit data unavailable today. What is most defensible?
questions.explanation: An option that needs unavailable visit data stays a hypothesis, contingent on obtaining that data. Calling the effect proven or the gap irrelevant ignores the gap, and visits cannot be estimated from transaction IDs.

options.label: Report the visitor effect as proven
Treat the data gap as irrelevant
Describe it as contingent on new evidence

questions.prompt: The manager wants to choose between immediate advertising and a coverage audit. What should guide the choice?
questions.explanation: The choice between advertising now and a coverage audit rests on whether recorded activity is comparable, because that decides whether the baseline can be trusted. Slide count, adjective count and the order in which the AI lists options are not evidence.

options.label: Which idea fits on fewer slides
The number of adjectives in the draft

questions.prompt: Two alternatives cite the same East total but propose opposite actions. What test is useful?
questions.explanation: When two options start from the same East total but recommend opposite actions, the difference lies in their assumptions. Compare each option's assumptions and the evidence for them. Blending the actions, hiding the conflict or choosing the more confident voice does not resolve it.

options.label: Compare each option's assumptions and evidence
Average the two actions into one plan
Choose the one with more confident language

questions.prompt: A store-coverage audit is feasible and informs all later options. Why might it come first?
questions.explanation: A coverage audit can show whether East's count is comparable, which reduces uncertainty for every later option. It does not give a profit margin, replace later business evaluation or guarantee growth.

options.label: It establishes a precise profit margin

questions.prompt: AI presents three actions but no evidence required to evaluate them. What is missing?
questions.explanation: An option without the information needed to test it cannot be prioritised or verified. Headings, extra paragraphs about AI or longer lists add volume but not decision logic.

options.label: A more formal heading for each action
An extra paragraph about AI capabilities
A longer list of unrelated activities
Testable information needs for each action

questions.prompt: A team must choose one next investigation. What makes its justification strongest?
questions.explanation: The strongest justification records the trade-off between what you expect to learn and the effort and feasibility of getting it. Promises of success, the AI's ranking or dismissing all other options are claims of authority, not reasons.

options.label: A recorded trade-off between value and feasibility
A promise that the chosen option will succeed
A choice based solely on the AI's ranking
A claim that all other options are useless

questions.prompt: East has the fewest recorded transactions, so the data show that East customers are less interested in buying and a promotion should be the next step.
questions.explanation: False. The count can reflect fewer stores, a shorter reporting window or lower activity, and the CSV cannot separate them. Comparable coverage has to be checked before the count is read as a demand problem or a promotion is chosen.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the Period 11 option process in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Options come first, from the verified diagnosis. Next they are compared in a table so evidence and assumptions are visible. The most attractive one is then challenged, and only after that does a person choose a direction and record the reasoning.
sequence: Generate three next-step options from the verified diagnosis
Compare them in a table of evidence, assumption and information needed
Challenge the most attractive option and name alternative explanations
A person chooses a direction and records the justification

questions.prompt: Match each option to the information it needs.
questions.explanation: A coverage check needs the store list, dates and extraction rules. A common-basis comparison needs store IDs, opening days and visits. Acquisition work needs traffic, conversion and campaign costs. A promotion proposal needs two alternative explanations that could be tested before any spending.

pairs.right: Store list, dates and extraction rules

pairs.left: Compare activity on a common basis
pairs.right: Store IDs, opening days and customer visits
Traffic or visits, conversion and campaign costs
Two alternative explanations and a check for each

lessons.title: Period 12 · Plan and Measure Action
lessons.description: Turn the chosen direction into actions, owners and deliverables, define success without inventing an uplift, assemble a one-page recommendation and save the investigation as a reusable prompt chain with a human pause.
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this period you can:
objectives: Turn a chosen direction into one action that names the information to obtain, why it is needed, a proposed role and a deliverable
Build a three-row action plan with owner, data or approval needed, deliverable and an observable success condition
Explain why transactions per operating store-day cannot be calculated from the current CSV
Write a one-page recommendation with a question, verified evidence, a limitation, a next action with proposed owner and a checkable outcome
Assemble the six-stage prompt chain and place the human pause before planning
Change one stage of a saved chain, such as a category comparison, without discarding checked work
lessons.body:
The manager has read your options table and approved one thing: **confirm comparable store and reporting coverage first.** Then comes the next question: "Fine. Who does what, and how will we know it worked?"

You cannot answer with a sales target, because the file contains none. What you can write is a plan whose actions, owners and outcomes are all **observable**, and a recommendation that ends honestly: the next step is to obtain better information.

> [!ghi-nho] An evidence-based decision process can sensibly end with a request for more reliable data. That is a result, not a failure to reach one.

:::Predict before you read
A colleague suggests the success measure "East net sales up 10% next quarter". Before reading on, write down what is wrong with it. Then think of a success measure for a coverage check that you could verify as done or not done.
:::

parts.md:
A useful action says **what** should be requested, **who** can provide or verify it, and **what output** resolves the question. Because the CSV has no store or date fields, the action is to *obtain new approved information*, not to manufacture a normalised metric from data you do not have. ```html
Action prompt
Turn the chosen direction, confirm comparable regional coverage, into one practical action. Name the necessary store and date information, why it is needed, the proposed responsible role, and the deliverable the retail manager will review. Leave timing and resources open for human confirmation.
``` **Why it works:** it asks for one action, not a programme. It leaves timing and resources open, so the AI cannot invent a deadline or a budget. An appropriate deliverable is a **documented coverage table**: which stores are represented, which reporting dates are included, which operating days are valid and which extraction rules were applied. With it, the manager can agree a scope for a fair comparison. > [!canh-bao] The lecture materials give a plan **example**. It is not a completed data acquisition or a store-level analysis, and your answers should not read as if it were.

```html
Follow-up — action plan
Expand this action into a short plan: action, proposed owner, data needed and deliverable. Ask about timing and resources that have not been agreed.
``` | Action | Proposed owner | Data or approval needed | Deliverable | Success condition | |---|---|---|---|---| | Confirm coverage | Data analyst or data owner | Store list, extraction dates, rules | Validated coverage summary | Comparable scope established, or gaps documented | | Compare activity fairly | Retail analyst | Store IDs, operating days, transaction counts | Activity comparison | Denominators and definitions checked | | Decide next action | Retail manager | The comparison and operational context | Approved next-step brief | Choice and reasoning documented | Proposed owners are **role examples, not assignments**. A real organisation must confirm roles, deadlines, resources and permitted sources. The plan should not state a fixed duration or a sales uplift, because neither is supplied. If coverage cannot be matched, the plan reports that constraint and proposes another way to obtain comparable data. **A future measure.** Once the data exist, a fair comparison metric would be *recorded transactions per operating store-day*: count transactions in a validated common scope and divide by the total store-days. For example, if validated data list each active store and its operating days for a common period, you could do exactly that. The current CSV supports none of it, since it has no store or day fields. Label the metric a **future measure**, never a current result.

sections.title: Define success and write the recommendation
sections.intro: Success is an observable deliverable: confirmed comparable store and date coverage, a valid activity denominator and a manager-approved next decision. A one-page recommendation has five elements.

parts.title: 1. A clear question
parts.md: What the manager needs to decide: should East's low count be treated as a business issue or a data issue?

parts.title: 2. Verified evidence
parts.md: East: 39 transactions, 182,004.38 net sales, 4,666.78 per transaction, from the CSV.

parts.title: 3. An unresolved limitation
parts.md: No store or date fields, so counts cannot be normalised for coverage.

parts.title: 4. A next action with proposed ownership
parts.md: A data analyst drafts a validated store-and-period inventory for the manager.

parts.title: 5. A checkable outcome
parts.md: A coverage summary exists and the manager can say whether a sales intervention needs further examination.

sections.outro:
```html
Final-briefing prompt
Combine the verified regional diagnosis, the human-approved decision to check coverage, and the action plan into a one-page management brief. Include the exact East transaction count, East net sales and East net sales per transaction, state the data limitation, identify proposed owners, and describe how the coverage check will support a subsequent decision. Keep hypotheses labelled.
``` **Why it works:** it asks for exact figures you can check, states the limitation as a required element, and keeps hypotheses labelled instead of letting them harden. **Brief excerpt.** East has 39 recorded transactions, 182,004.38 in net sales and 4,666.78 in net sales per recorded transaction. This is the smallest recorded total and the highest per-transaction value among the regions. The file lacks stores and dates, so observed counts cannot be normalised for coverage. Request a validated store-and-period inventory before evaluating East's transaction activity. A retail manager reviews the comparable summary and decides whether commercial action is necessary. It is reasonable to recommend **an investigation** rather than a promotion when key evidence is absent.

sections.title: The reusable six-stage chain
sections.intro: Periods 10 to 12 follow one logic that you can save as a template. It works inside the course cycle (Define, Design, Execute, Evaluate, Refine) and does not replace it.

parts.title: 1. Explore
parts.md: Calculate checked regional net sales, counts and net sales per transaction, and reconcile all totals.

parts.title: 2. Visualise and break down
parts.md: Plot or specify suitable comparisons, then examine one selected region by product category.

parts.title: 3. Diagnose
parts.md: Give verified findings, alternative explanations and missing data.

parts.title: 4. Develop options
parts.md: Present three next steps with evidence, assumptions and required new information. Challenge the leading option.

parts.title: 5. Pause for human choice
parts.md: The AI recommends a direction and then **waits** for your explicit confirmation.

parts.title: 6. Plan and summarise
parts.md: Only after you confirm: actions, proposed owners, data requests, deliverables and success measures, then a one-page draft.

sections.outro:
```html
Reusable Case 2 chain
You are helping a retail manager investigate one priority using an approved transaction CSV. First confirm the decision question, source, audience and success criteria. Ask only for missing information that changes the task.
1. EXPLORE. Calculate checked regional net sales, transaction counts and net sales per transaction. Reconcile all totals.
2. VISUALISE AND BREAK DOWN. Plot or specify suitable comparisons, then examine one selected region by product category.
3. DIAGNOSE. Give verified findings, alternative explanations and missing data.
4. DEVELOP OPTIONS. Present three next steps with evidence, assumptions and required new information. Challenge the leading option.
5. PAUSE. Recommend a direction, then wait for my explicit confirmation.
6. PLAN AND SUMMARISE. Only after confirmation, create actions, proposed owners, data requests, deliverables and success measures. Draft one page.
Never invent currency, dates, store counts, profit or causal explanations. Keep intermediate evidence accessible and stop if a critical check fails.
``` **What makes it good:** stages 1 to 3 repeat Period 10, stage 4 repeats Period 11 and stage 6 is this period. The last line is the safety rail: it forbids the exact inventions this module warns against and tells the AI to stop when a check fails. > [!canh-bao] The written pause is only a request. If your chatbot cannot reliably stop inside one long prompt, split the chain into separate turns and send stage 6 only after you have approved the direction.

sections.title: Reuse the chain: revise, decide, save time

parts.md:
**Revise one stage without starting again.** Suppose the manager now wants Electronics compared across regions. Change only the relevant stage and keep the work you have verified. ```html
Targeted revision
Keep the checked regional totals. For Stage 2, compare Electronics transaction counts and net sales by region. Update the diagnosis and options to reflect that comparison. Preserve unsupported explanations as hypotheses and pause again before Stage 6.
``` A new grouping must be verified independently. Recalculated from the CSV: | Region | Electronics transactions | Electronics net sales | Per transaction | |---|---|---|---| | East | 4 | 10,559.24 | 2,639.81 | | North | 16 | 81,249.22 | 5,078.08 | | South | 14 | 68,454.87 | 4,889.63 | | West | 12 | 39,549.82 | 3,295.82 | | **All regions** | **46** | **199,813.15** | **4,343.76** | East has 4 Electronics records against 12 to 16 elsewhere, and Electronics is 10.3% of East's records against 23.5% to 28.1% in the other regions. That sharpens the question, but it still does not say why. If the new comparison changes your recommended direction, the person who chose the direction must **approve it again**. **Decide and plan.** Stages 4 to 6 are the continuation: develop options with data needs and assumptions, stop and request the manager's choice, and only after confirmation plan the actions, owners, data and measures. Keep the checked regional and East category figures in view throughout. **Save time safely.** To reuse the reviewed chain on a similar question, replace the task brief and the source file. Each run must inspect the input, **recalculate** the summaries and record new limitations. Previously recorded outputs must never be carried over as if they described the new data. A reusable prompt reduces drafting work; you still test the outputs and approve business actions. A scheduled run is optional and needs access to approved input files and human review.

parts.title: Is a plan that ends in "get more data" too weak for a manager?
parts.md: Not if it says exactly which data, who obtains them, what the deliverable is and how the manager will use it. It prevents the much more expensive mistake of spending on an intervention that addresses a data difference.

parts.title: Can the AI name the real owner and the deadline?
parts.md: It can propose roles and a timeline, clearly marked as proposals. The organisation confirms real people, deadlines and resources. The AI should ask about anything not agreed instead of inventing it.

parts.title: What if the chatbot gives a polished plan but one figure in it is unchecked?
parts.md: Hold approval until the figure is verified. A material unchecked input may change the recommended action, and a clear narrative does not make a number correct.

parts.title: My chain worked for East. Can I run it for North?
parts.md: Run it again with North as the input and recheck every output. The instructions are reusable; the East numbers and conclusions are not.

sections.title: Check it yourself, then do Activity 3

parts.md:
1. Build a three-row action plan for East with roles, inputs and observable outcomes. Make sure no row contains a sales target, deadline or budget you invented.
2. Explain in one sentence why transactions per store-day cannot be computed from the current file.
3. Write a 120-word brief with one verified observation, one limitation and one next step. Check every figure against the CSV.
4. Pick a different product category and edit the chain to study it while keeping the data checks.

:::Find the error
An AI-drafted brief says: "East is weak. The AI assistant will launch a 10% promotion on Monday and expect sales to rise by next quarter. Store coverage is probably fine, so no check is needed."

Find at least four problems before you open this box.
:::

:::Open the solution after you have tried
1. "East is weak" is a verdict on total alone; East's value per transaction is the highest.
2. "The AI assistant will launch" gives the AI the decision. A person must approve any action with real-world effects.
3. "Expect sales to rise" is an unsupported uplift claim. The file has no baseline, cost or experiment.
4. "Coverage is probably fine" is an unverified assumption, and it is the very thing the chosen direction was meant to check.
:::

> [!ghi-nho] **Activity 3** puts the whole chain into practice on the CSV: regional and East tables with an independent spreadsheet check, an evidence ledger, a three-option matrix, your own decision, an action plan and a one-page recommendation. Open the **Assignments** tab of this lesson to submit it.

items.meaning: Activities with proposed owners, required information, deliverables and success conditions.
A role example, such as data analyst or retail manager, that the organisation must confirm. It is not an assignment made by the AI.
The output someone will review, such as a validated coverage summary or an approved next-step brief.
An observable condition showing that an action is complete, not an invented uplift target.
items.example: Comparable store and date coverage is confirmed, or the gaps are documented.

items.meaning: A metric that needs data you do not have yet, and so must not be reported as a current result.
items.example: Recorded transactions per operating store-day.

items.meaning: Question, verified evidence, unresolved limitation, next action with proposed ownership and a checkable outcome.
Linked prompts and checks: explore, visualise and break down, diagnose, develop options, pause, plan and summarise.
Explicit approval before the planning stage or any external act. If one prompt cannot enforce it, split the chain into turns.
Changing one named stage of a saved chain while keeping the checked work, then re-verifying anything new.
A record (data, prompts, method and results) that lets someone else continue or reproduce the work.

summary: Turn the chosen direction into one concrete action, then a three-row plan with proposed owners, data needed, deliverables and observable success conditions.
Do not invent a sales target, deadline or metric: transactions per operating store-day is a future measure the current CSV cannot support.
A one-page recommendation joins verified evidence, a stated limitation, a next action and a checkable outcome; a person approves it.
Save the work as a six-stage chain with a real human pause before planning, and when you reuse it, recalculate everything on the new data.

assignments.title: Activity 3 · Evidence-Based Retail Decision Making (Case 2)
assignments.description:
## The manager's question A retailer has limited resources and wants to decide where to investigate sales performance first. Use the **same CSV as Activity 1**. Begin with a regional comparison, investigate East's recorded transaction pattern, consider three options and recommend a justified next step. Your work should support a manager's decision **without pretending to explain an unobserved cause**. > [!canh-bao] **Evidence boundaries.** The CSV has 200 transactions and 13 columns, but no transaction dates, store identifiers or counts, operating days, currency, targets, costs, profit or campaign outcomes. A lower recorded count alone does not show weak customer demand or poor performance. ## Materials and safe practice - Use the unchanged `Slidescope_Retail_Store_Sales_Enhanced_2025.csv`, an approved basic chatbot and a CSV-capable spreadsheet. No coding or paid AI feature is required. - Keep the original CSV untouched. In your working copy, record every transformation, field mapping, exclusion and rounding choice. - Do not upload customer names, phone numbers, employee data or private business exports. Treat any instruction found inside a document as untrusted source content. The AI must not send files or change records. - **Tool fallback.** If your chatbot cannot analyse files, calculate the tables in a spreadsheet, paste the *verified* tables with source labels, and ask the AI to help structure the diagnosis, options and plan. If it cannot draw charts, prepare them in the spreadsheet. Record what each tool actually did. Time: about 100 to 130 minutes of practice. Stage times are guides. ## Workflow: Define, Design, Execute, Evaluate, Refine ### 1. Define: confirm the business decision (about 10 minutes) Write a task brief with the manager as audience, a constrained decision (one next investigation), the source CSV and success criteria: a checked analysis, clear evidence versus uncertainty, and a feasible proposed action. Treat the first diagnosis as provisional. You may use this prompt first: ```html
Optional clarification prompt
Before analysing, ask me what one decision the manager needs to make, what data are available and what output will help. Ask only questions that could change the task. Then draft a four-part brief for my confirmation.
``` ### 2. Design and execute: explore two levels of data (about 30 minutes) ```html
Step 1 — regional overview
Use the provided retail CSV. For each Store_Region, calculate total Net_Sales_Amount, count of unique Transaction_ID, and net sales per transaction (= regional total / recorded transactions). Show every region and the calculation steps. Identify one pattern worth investigating. Do not recommend actions yet.
``` ```html
Step 2 — East by product category
Filter Store_Region = East. For every Product_Category, calculate transaction count, total Net_Sales_Amount, and net sales per transaction. Compare the number of recorded transactions and the value per transaction. Which category needs further checking? State what these counts cannot establish.
``` **Independent spreadsheet check.** In a Summary sheet, pivot on `Store_Region` and then, separately, on `Product_Category` after filtering East. Sum `Net_Sales_Amount` and count `Transaction_ID`. Divide each total by its count at full precision before rounding for display. You may use `COUNTIFS` and `SUMIFS` instead. **Stop and check.** Before asking AI to diagnose causes, verify the eight group figures, the four-region total and whether unique transaction IDs agree with the row counts. Correct any discrepancy and keep the calculation record. ### 3. Evaluate: separate observations from possible explanations (about 15 minutes) ```html
Step 3 — working diagnosis
Write a short diagnosis using only the verified tables. Label each statement VERIFIED FACT, INTERPRETATION, HYPOTHESIS or DATA NEEDED. Suggest at least two possible explanations for East's recorded pattern. Explain why the CSV cannot prove either explanation. End with one question for the manager.
``` Complete an **evidence ledger** with at least three entries (claim or question, label, source or check, or the missing evidence) before you choose an option. A fact is something the CSV and your calculation directly establish; a hypothesis requires additional evidence. ### 4. Design and evaluate: challenge three options (about 20 minutes) ```html
Step 4 — option matrix
Suggest three possible next steps, including a check of store/reporting coverage and one intervention someone might propose. For each, show supporting evidence, the unconfirmed assumption, and additional data required. Challenge the suggestion "Run a promotion to increase East transactions." Give two alternative explanations for the lower recorded count.
``` Record the three options in a table with the columns **Option, Verified evidence, Assumption, Data needed**. > [!ghi-nho] **Human decision gate.** Stop here. You act as the manager: choose a direction and write a two-sentence justification. Do not let the chatbot approve its own recommended action. If the evidence is insufficient, choose a data-checking step and explain why. ### 5. Refine: turn your chosen direction into a plan (about 20 minutes) ```html
Steps 5 and 6 — plan after my approval
I choose [your direction] because [verified evidence + uncertainty]. Draft a short plan: action, proposed owner, additional data, deliverable and measurable success criterion. Ask about unagreed timing and resources. Then write a one-page recommendation separating evidence, uncertainty, the approved next step and what the manager should decide after reviewing the new data. Draft only; do not send or change records.
``` A completion criterion should be testable (for example, whether comparable coverage can be established), not an invented uplift target. Owner, deadline and resource proposals remain subject to manager approval. ### 6. Evidence and handover (about 15 minutes) Describe a folder such as `Retail_Review_East/` containing `01_data` (unaltered CSV), `02_prompts` (final chain and meaningful follow-ups), `03_analysis` (spreadsheet, charts and `method_note.txt`), `04_final` (reviewed one-page recommendation) and `README.txt` (dataset version, task and file locations). If project tools are unavailable, ordinary local folders work. The documentation habits behind this folder are taught in Periods 13 and 14. ## What to submit Submit one text response containing, in this order: 1. **Task brief** (audience, decision, source, success criteria). 2. **Regional table** and **East category table** (group, transactions, total net sales, net sales per transaction), with one line stating how you verified them independently in the spreadsheet. 3. **Evidence ledger** with at least three entries, each labelled VERIFIED FACT, INTERPRETATION, HYPOTHESIS or DATA NEEDED. 4. **Option matrix** with three options, and your challenge of the promotion suggestion with two alternative explanations. 5. **Your chosen direction** and a two-sentence justification, written by you. 6. **Action plan** (action, proposed owner, data needed, deliverable, measurable success criterion) and the **one-page recommendation**. 7. **Prompt trail and method note**: your final chain, the follow-ups that mattered, which tool was used, run conditions, the source filename and your rounding choices. 8. **Handover folder structure**, plus a statement of how a peer could reproduce East's transaction count and net sales without the chatbot. 9. **Reflection**, in a few sentences each: (a) Does East's smaller recorded count establish weak demand? What comparison would be needed? (b) What could go wrong if a promotion starts before comparable store and date coverage is established? (c) What would your peer need to reproduce the recommendation if your chat history disappeared? ## Checklist before you submit - Regional and East-category tables, with a source-based independent spreadsheet verification. - Evidence ledger separating fact, interpretation, hypothesis and missing information. - Three-option comparison and an explicit promotion challenge. - Human-approved direction and a one-page recommendation with action, proposed owner, data, deliverable and success criterion. - Full prompt trail, run conditions, source filename, method note and handover folder structure. - A peer or reviewer could reproduce East's count and net sales without the chatbot.
assignments.rubricText:
Practice rubric (from the Activity 3 Student sheet). Score each of the five criteria 0, 1 or 2; the practice total is out of 10. A formal course weighting is not specified.

0 = missing or incorrect. 1 = partly met. 2 = fully met.

1. Task and workflow (0-2). 2 points: connected prompts follow the manager's decision and preserve the human pause.
2. Calculation and evidence (0-2). 2 points: regional and category checks are reproducible and correct against the source CSV.
3. Reasoning (0-2). 2 points: facts, hypotheses and missing inputs are clearly distinguished.
4. Options and decision (0-2). 2 points: three compared options, the promotion challenged, and a defensible choice made by the learner.
5. Action and handover (0-2). 2 points: a practical action with owner, data and outcome, and a complete working record.

Things to look for: no invented currency, dates, store counts, profit, uplift targets or causes; evidence boundaries respected; calculations done at full precision before rounding; the learner, not the chatbot, approves the direction; a peer could reproduce East's count and net sales without the chatbot.

questions.prompt: Who owns the final approval of an AI-assisted action plan?
questions.explanation: A responsible person keeps decision authority. The AI drafts, formulas calculate and a template repeats a process, but none of them is accountable for approving an operational action.

questions.prompt: An action plan says “Check coverage.” What addition makes it executable?
questions.explanation: "Check coverage" becomes executable when it names who does it, what inputs they need and when it is due, with the deadline proposed by the AI and confirmed by the manager. Praise, a fancier role prompt or another causal claim tell nobody what to do.

questions.prompt: What is a success measure used for?
questions.explanation: A success measure is an observable test of whether an action achieved what it was meant to. It does not hide uncertainty, prove that a campaign caused a result or replace the original goal.

questions.prompt: A coverage audit aims to compare regional activity fairly. Which output indicates completion?
questions.explanation: The audit's aim is a fair comparison, so completion looks like a verified comparison of stores and dates. An unlabelled chart, a predicted profit rise or a claim that demand has recovered says nothing about whether coverage was matched.

options.label: A verified comparison of stores and dates
A predicted profit rise in East
A claim that demand has recovered

questions.prompt: The recommendation contains a diagnosis and action but no evidence. What should be added?
questions.explanation: A manager needs to trace the diagnosis to a checked figure and its source, for example East's 39 transactions and 182,004.38 net sales from the CSV. Testimonials, claims of success or text about the chatbot add persuasion but no evidence.

options.label: A checked figure with its data source
A longer description of the chatbot
A strong claim of immediate success

questions.prompt: Why use a connected prompt chain in the business case?
questions.explanation: A chain carries checked outputs from one stage to the next so you do not rebuild the context each time. It does not guarantee a good decision, replace the checking of intermediate results or remove the human.

options.label: To carry verified outputs between stages

questions.prompt: Before AI drafts the final plan, the manager must choose a direction. Where should the workflow pause?
questions.explanation: The pause belongs after the options have been compared and before planning, so a person chooses the direction the plan will serve. Pausing before the task exists, at an irrelevant event or after publication would reverse the control.

options.label: Only when the report file is deleted

questions.prompt: A reusable chain works for East but is later applied to North. What must be changed?
questions.explanation: A reusable chain keeps its instructions but must be re-run on the new inputs, with every figure recalculated. East's numbers and recommendations describe East's data and do not carry over to North.

options.label: Copy East's recommendations word for word
Assume earlier findings apply to North
Replace the region inputs and recheck outputs

questions.prompt: An operational plan names a data analyst as owner. What else should the plan specify?
questions.explanation: Naming an owner is only useful if the plan says what evidence that person must deliver. Invented benchmarks, guarantees of success and a model persona are not deliverables.

options.label: A fabricated benchmark for every store
The evidence the analyst must deliver

questions.prompt: A manager compares results before and after an intervention, but store coverage differs. What is the main caution?
questions.explanation: If store coverage differs between the two periods, a change may come from the coverage rather than the intervention. Compare on matching coverage before drawing a conclusion. A chatbot cannot verify causation, and nothing here shows a currency change.

options.label: The comparison may reflect coverage changes

questions.prompt: What should a one-page management recommendation include?
questions.explanation: A one-page recommendation links verified evidence to a chosen action and to a way of reviewing the outcome. Raw chat logs, colour palettes and unsupported causes break that chain.

options.label: All raw chatbot messages without summary
Only the final chart's color palette
Evidence, chosen action and review measure
A list of unsupported business causes

questions.prompt: A prompt-based chain suggests a customer-facing policy change. What control is essential?
questions.explanation: A model-generated proposal is not an approval. A change with real-world consequences, such as a customer-facing policy, needs accountable human authorisation, and the data limitations must stay visible.

options.label: Allow AI to publish the policy immediately
Treat the suggestion as an approved rule

questions.prompt: The workflow generates a compelling recommendation while one calculation remains unchecked. How should it proceed?
questions.explanation: If an unchecked figure might change the recommended action, hold approval until it is verified. A clear narrative does not make a number correct, and removing the figure while claiming it was checked is worse.

options.label: Assume one error cannot affect the choice
Remove the figure and claim it was checked
Approve it because the narrative is clear
Hold approval until the figure is verified

questions.prompt: Put the six stages of the reusable Case 2 chain in the correct order.
questions.explanation: The chain runs from the checked overview to the plan. The pause for human choice comes after options have been developed and challenged, and before any planning, so a person decides what the plan will serve.
sequence: Explore: checked regional totals, counts and net sales per transaction
Visualise and break down: compare regions, then examine one region by category
Diagnose: verified findings, alternatives and missing data
Develop options: three next steps, with the leading option challenged
Pause: recommend a direction and wait for explicit human confirmation
Plan and summarise: actions, owners, data requests, measures and a one-page draft

questions.prompt: A new comparison groups the full 200-row CSV by Electronics only. How many Electronics transactions are recorded in the North region?
questions.explanation: North has 16 Electronics transactions, against 4 in East, 14 in South and 12 in West (46 in all). A new grouping like this one must be verified independently in the spreadsheet, and a different pattern in the comparison could change the recommended direction and require renewed approval.

questions.prompt: The comparison metric "recorded transactions per operating store-day" can be calculated from the current CSV.
questions.explanation: False. The CSV has no store or date fields, so there is no store count or operating-day count to divide by. It is a future measure that needs validated store and day information.

modules.title: Module 5 — Privacy, Security, Documentation and Reproducibility
modules.description: Two periods on using AI so that others can trust, check and repeat your work. Period 13 covers unsupported claims, limiting what you share, untrusted content in documents, and control of access and actions. Period 14 covers the working record, project organisation, method notes, linking claims to evidence and peer reproduction. Includes the Module 5 lecture notes, slides, activity sheet and dataset.

lessons.title: Module 5 materials: lecture notes, slides, activity sheet and dataset
lessons.description: What is attached to Module 5 (Periods 13 and 14), which section and which slides match each part of the two lessons, and how to use them.
lessons.body:
Module 5 closes the course. Its two periods ask a different question from the earlier ones. Not "how do I get a good answer?" but "can someone else trust this work, check it and repeat it?" The files below cover the whole module.

## What is attached

- **Lecture notes (PDF, whole course).** One document for all 14 periods. For this module read Period 13 (sections 13.1 to 13.5) and Period 14 (sections 14.1 to 14.6). Each period ends with key concepts, a summary and five review questions. The glossary and the reference list are at the end of the document.
- **Slides, 150 pages (PDF).** The full deck. Module 5 is pages 128 to 148.
- **Slides, 81 pages (PDF).** The shorter deck: Period 13 is pages 66 to 71 and Period 14 is pages 72 to 79. It has no checkpoint or takeaway slides.
